The Robbins-Siegmund theorem establishes the convergence of stochastic processes that are almost supermartingales and is one of the most commonly used approaches for analyzing stochastic iterative algorithms in stochastic approximation and reinforcement learning (RL). However, its original form has a significant limitation as it requires the zero-order term to be summable. In many important RL applications, this summable condition, however, cannot be met. This limitation motivates us to extend the Robbins-Siegmund theorem for almost supermartingales where the zero-order term is not summable, but only square-summable. In particular, we introduce a novel and mild assumption on the increments of the stochastic processes. This together with the square-summable condition enables an almost sure convergence to a bounded set. Additionally, we further provide almost sure convergence rates, high probability concentration bounds, and $L^p$ convergence rates. We then apply the new results to stochastic approximation and RL. Notably, we obtain the first almost sure convergence rate, the first high probability concentration bound, and the first $L^p$ convergence rate for $Q$-learning with linear function approximation.

We further develop a Deep BSDE method combining reflected-path simulation, geometry-aware boundary treatment, and efficient evaluation of the constrained Hamiltonian. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the method, providing a mesh-free framework for high-dimensional constrained portfolio problems with Neumann boundary.

These results demonstrate the effectiveness of Benders cut filtering on this problem class and motivate evaluation in other domains.

This paper is complemented by the companion paper [Fornasier, Klemenc, Scagliotti, "A Lions Lift Framework for Gradient and Newtonian Evolutions in Wasserstein spaces"], which specifies and adapts the results to the Wasserstein metric space $(\mathcal{P}_2,W_2)$ through Lions lift, which explains Vlasov equations as Newtonian flows on spaces of probability measures.

An agent's probability report is paid for twice: by a strictly proper scoring rule, which rewards accuracy, and by an approval rule for the decision it triggers. An approval rule that is not affine is known to defeat truthful reporting. We show the conflict is built in: whenever perfect screening is attainable, the welfare-maximizing approval rule is never affine. The distortion is predictable: there is a reserve report at which pretending to be the marginal type costs exactly what approval is worth. Approving every report at or above the reserve sorts agents as if their beliefs were observed, under every strictly proper score and for any belief distribution. So does a continuous rule with one corner; under strict feasibility no continuously differentiable rule does. The binding constraint is steepness, not smoothness: a slope-capped rule sorts perfectly if and only if the cap reaches the critical slope, the steepest chord of the pretending cost up to the reserve; below it the welfare loss is cubic in the shortfall. For the Brier, log and power scores, and whenever the pretending cost is convex up to the reserve, the critical slope has a closed form. The instances are AI-agent oversight and marketplace operation.

Joint analysis avoids this dependence on decision order, but combinatorial growth has historically made it prohibitive in large cases. We reduce the search using genetic compatibility tests, likelihood-based pruning of unlikely assignments, and symmetry reductions. Together, these advances yield a manageable set of candidate assignments and their likelihoods, from which we construct an integer linear program that resolves competing identifications and determines the global maximum-likelihood assignment. In small benchmarks, the method recovers the exhaustive-search optimum with up to 99.96% fewer likelihood evaluations. We also apply it to simulated disasters involving up to 10 thousand victims and missing persons. The framework is not limited to a single global optimum but yields a list of probable alternative assignments, thus providing a flexible tool to be used alongside other forensic evidence.

Dynamic pricing with resource constraints requires balancing exploration of unknown demand patterns against exploitation of known information to maximize revenue. In the full-information setting, a residual-correction policy that solves the fluid problem once attains $O(\log T)$ regret with bounded prices and arbitrary-rank resource matrices. In the no-information setting, deterministic exploration followed by a certainty-equivalent policy attains $O(\sqrt T)$ regret when the limiting fluid solution is nondegenerate. In the informed-price setting, given an initial price-demand estimate, a feedback controller learns the implementing prices without estimating the slope matrix if the slope matrix is symmetric, a set containing it is known in advance, the informed price is aligned with the resource constraints, and an inverse-image condition holds. A selector chooses between the informed-price algorithm and the no-information algorithm from historical data. Its regret bound includes observation error, misalignment, inventory exits, and periods on the fixed price. We further show how offline surrogate models reduce the regret of the learning policy through variance reduction, even when misspecified. The bound includes calibration and screen failures, and the regret is reduced for all sufficiently large horizons. We finally demonstrate the empirical performances of our policies through complete numerical experiments.

We investigate the nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation associated with anisotropic consensus-based optimization. Under suitable assumptions on the objective function, we establish global existence and uniqueness of density valued weak solutions for bounded initial probability densities with finite fourth moment. The main analytical challenge arises from the component-wise degeneracy of the diffusion, which vanishes along moving coordinate hyperplanes determined by the weighted consensus point. To overcome this difficulty, we develop spatial translation estimates based on weighted gradient bounds and uniform density estimates. Combined with temporal translation and moment estimates, these yield strong compactness in $L^2((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^d)$ through the Fréchet--Kolmogorov compactness criterion, enabling passage to the limit in the regularized equations. Uniqueness is established through the associated McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equation and Wasserstein stability of the weighted consensus point. Furthermore, we prove the propagation of $H^2$-regularity for sufficiently regular initial data.

To establish these guarantees, we construct a computable lower bound on the zero-setup optimal cost by tracking units already on hand or committed for delivery. We then combine it with a bound on holding and setup costs required by batching to obtain the general-setup guarantee and instance-specific performance bounds for any admissible replenishment policy. In our numerical study, the largest estimated policy-cost-to-lower-bound ratios are about $1.59$ for our heuristic $(r, Q)$ policy and $1.47$ after joint optimization of $r$ and $Q$. The heuristic also performs well against the optimized policy: over the sampled instances, its median extra cost ranges from $2.33\%$ to $3.91\%$, depending on the setup cost.

Gradient descent (GD) is one of the most fundamental algorithms in optimization. Yet even for smooth convex objectives, the optimal rate among predetermined nonnegative stepsize schedules has remained unresolved. Altschuler and Parrilo [Mathematical Programming, 2025] showed that their recursive silver stepsize schedule achieves an $O(n^{-p_{\mathrm{sil}}})$ rate, where $p_{\mathrm{sil}}=\log_2(1+\sqrt2)\approx1.2716$, improving upon the classical $O(n^{-1})$ rate of constant-step GD. Although the optimality of $p_{\mathrm{sil}}$ has been well supported by numerical evidence for small $n$, a matching lower bound has remained missing. In this paper, we prove an $Ω(n^{-p_{\mathrm{sil}}-o(1)})$ lower bound for GD, showing that $p_{\mathrm{sil}}$ is the optimal convergence exponent. Additionally, we prove an anytime lower bound that matches the exponent $2p_{\mathrm{sil}}/(1+p_{\mathrm{sil}})\approx1.1195$ of the known upper bound [Zhang, Lee, Du, and Chen, COLT 2025]. Building on the approaches of [Ma and Chen, 2026; Jung, Cho, and Yun, 2026], we select specific iterations as checkpoints at which the GD trajectory explores a new coordinate, and we couple these coordinates using a chain of local functions. Our main technical contribution is a local hard function that bends the GD trajectory between successive checkpoints, resulting in a sharpened lower bound. For each prescribed stepsize schedule, we maximize this bound over admissible checkpoint sets. A recursive analysis of this maximum then yields a lower bound matching the silver exponent for every such schedule.

For nonconvex objectives or unknown problem parameters, we further consider an adaptive restart variant with proximal gradient safeguards. If the initial sublevel set is compact, we prove that every accumulation point of the safeguard reference sequence is stationary and that an $\varepsilon$-stationary point is obtained within $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ iterations for any tolerance $\varepsilon>0$. Both methods also apply to smooth objectives. In this setting, the basic method yields a single Riemannian accelerated gradient scheme for geodesically convex and geodesically $μ$-strongly convex problems. Its iteration and parameter recurrence extend continuously to $μ=0$, and a single analysis establishes accelerated rates in both cases. Numerical experiments on nonsmooth composite and smooth problems demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

♻ ☆ A Projection-Free Algorithm for Variational Inequalities in Hilbert Spaces with Strong Convergence

We study variational inequalities governed by a point-to-set maximal monotone operator in a real Hilbert space and constrained by a convex inequality \(C=\{x\in\Hi:c(x)\le0\}\), where the defining function \(c\) is continuous and not necessarily differentiable. The proposed method uses only projections onto intersections of half-spaces and avoids the metric projection onto \(C\). Feasibility is handled by subgradient cuts and, when a trial operator point is infeasible, by a Slater correction based on a fixed strictly feasible point. The variational inequality is represented by Minty-type separating half-spaces generated at feasible graph points of the operator, and a Haugazeau half-space is added to obtain best-approximation convergence. Under a Slater-corrected feasible-separation condition, together with explicit exact, approximate and finite-candidate oracle realisations, the whole sequence converges strongly to \(P_{S^*}(x^0)\), the projection of the initial point onto the solution set. We also derive best-iterate \(O(N^{-1/2})\) residual estimates for the step residual, feasibility violation and Minty gap. The analysis is stated directly for point-to-set maximal monotone operators, while the concrete oracle realisations include finite-dimensional single-valued models. We record the consequences of strong monotonicity in the point-to-set setting and provide numerical comparisons on nonsmooth and large-scale constraints, including maxima of convex quadratics, a discretised optimal-control problem, mixed-norm sparse recovery, a Cournot--Nash capacity equilibrium, and a genuine point-to-set \(\ell_1\)-subdifferential example.

☆ Plan your Self-Adaptation! Ontology-Mediated Task and Architecture Co-adaptation Planning for Robots

Autonomous robots may need to adapt both their task plans and architectural configurations as operating conditions change. These decisions are interdependent: architectural configurations determine which actions a robot can perform, while task plans determine which capabilities are required. This paper presents PLANTA, an ontology-mediated approach to task and architecture co-adaptation that considers these dependencies during mission planning. PLANTA uses an ontology expressed in the Web Ontology Language to represent architectural alternatives and their associated functional and quality requirements, while the Planning Domain Definition Language defines task actions and mission goals. By automatically translating and integrating these models, PLANTA enables joint planning of task and reconfiguration actions. The approach uses satisficing planning and replans when changes during execution invalidate the current plan. PLANTA is evaluated in two robotic scenarios involving underwater inspection and ground navigation. The results support the feasibility of runtime co-adaptation and show lower planning time and memory consumption compared with optimal-policy generation in the evaluated navigation scenario, while producing plans of similar quality.

Anthony Longo
Crisis and disaster governance increasingly relies on technologies that sense, classify and act faster than humans can. Drone swarms coordinated with human operators, known as human-swarm teaming, provide a productive case to review the field of crisis governance. They promise better situational awareness in disaster response, but they also raise questions about human control, responsibility, surveillance, triage, dual use and public legitimacy. This report maps the ethical and societal territory that HST opens up. It unpacks this territory with a 3i-framework, the Interface, where operators and swarms work together, the Infrastructure, where organisations distribute tasks, decisions and blame, and the Imaginary, where law, policy and shared societal assumptions define what a crisis is and which interventions it justifies. The central claim is that these concerns cannot be addressed one level at a time. Many of the most pressing problems, such as responsibility gaps and the erosion of meaningful human control, arise at the joints between levels, through four translations, habits harden, routines become stories, principles become procedures, and procedures become prompts. Drawing on a critical review of literature across philosophy of technology, political theory, moral psychology, philosophy of mind, AI ethics, and critical disaster and security studies, the report develops this framework, illustrates it with two worked examples, and derives design and governance implications and a set of questions for developers, emergency organisations and policymakers.

These predictions are compared with the measured gas pattern to update a probabilistic belief over the source location. As the wind field is reconstructed incrementally, the framework also accounts for the spatially non-uniform reliability of wind field estimation and its influence on the source estimation. The resulting belief map is then used for informative path planning to guide the robot toward informative regions. High-fidelity simulations provide a comprehensive evaluation of the individual components and their integrations within the complete system, while physical indoor experiments assess the system performance under realistic sensing, motion, and airflow conditions. The results demonstrate that incorporating lightweight physical knowledge significantly improves localization robustness under spatially complex airflow and enables more efficient exploration.

☆ Infer3D: Inverse Generative Modeling Enables Robust 3D Reconstruction

Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy. In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

Finally, Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions, linking scene evolution with action generation. Moreover, Phoenix maintains high success rates when adapted with limited downstream demonstrations, demonstrating strong few-shot adaptation. Our code, pretraining data, and models are available on the project page to help the community reproduce our results.

General-purpose reward models demonstrate broad task transfer, but transfer from short-task pretraining to long-horizon tasks remains underexplored. Long-horizon progress models often rely on task-specific subtask classifiers or fixed action vocabularies, limiting the reuse of learned progress knowledge when adapting to new tasks. To address these challenges, we introduce Grana, a vision-language robot reward model that learns to identify unfinished subtasks and estimate their continuous progress using open-vocabulary subtask descriptions. For long-horizon tasks, we combine the selected subtask's predicted progress with credit for preceding completed subtasks to estimate whole-task progress. General progress prediction requires training the model across diverse tasks with progress supervision that accounts for imperfect execution. Elapsed-time proxies can misrepresent progress when relative subtask durations vary, or failures reverse local progress. We therefore introduce an annotation protocol that converts sparse subtask boundaries and action-quality annotations into dense progress targets, without requiring annotators to assign numerical progress scores. Pretraining with this supervision on 200 diverse, mostly short-horizon manipulation tasks enables zero-shot reward prediction on unseen tasks and improves progress prediction after adaptation to multi-minute, long-horizon tasks. Experiments demonstrate (i) generalizable reward prediction, including adaptation to five long-horizon tasks, (ii) benefits from pretraining and composing subtask progress estimates, and (iii) improved downstream policy performance.

Recent work on human-scene interaction (HSI) generation moves from single interactions to long-horizon interaction, where a language-model agent plans and executes a sequence of interactions in a 3D scene under one instruction. However, existing agents struggle in challenging everyday scenarios (e.g., picking up a toy and throwing it into a basket) because they lack spatial control over the motion and quantitative feedback on its execution, and they often fail to complete the interaction sequence. To address these gaps, we present Inhabitant, a training-free agent framework in which the agent specifies each motion through positions, paths and poses, measures how the executed interaction deviates from its intent, and revises the control specification accordingly. For an extensive evaluation in such scenarios, we build Inhabit, a benchmark of 75 household tasks in 31 furniture layouts of an apartment, in which every task chains one to three goals on movable objects and is carried out by the whole body, excluding fingers. On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7\% of the tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, and 93.3\% and 82.7\% with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, respectively. Ablations confirm that without spatial control the agent fails most tasks, and without quantitative feedback its motion becomes less precise. Code is available on the project page.

Robotic haircutting requires accurate motion execution and reliable communication to safely reproduce the operator's commands. Internet-based teleoperation is a key enabling technology to remotely perform precise manipulation tasks such as haircutting. However, communication uncertainties, including variable transmission delays and packet jitter, degrade synchronization between the master and slave systems and affect tracking performance. This paper presents a unilateral Internet teleoperation framework for robotic haircutting that takes into account experimentally measured communication uncertainties. Three delay-compensation techniques, namely Zero-Order Hold (ZOH), First-Order Hold (FOH), and Low-Pass Filtering (LPF), are evaluated together with a classical proportional-derivative (PD) controller and a passivity-based synchronization controller. Unlike conventional studies based on synthetic delay models, the proposed framework is validated using communication data acquired from a real cloud-based teleoperation platform, where both packet delay and effective delay are characterized. The results demonstrate that combining delay-compensation techniques with passivity-based synchronization improves the robustness of unilateral Internet teleoperation under realistic communication uncertainties, providing a reliable control framework for robotic haircutting applications.

Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.

Without fine-tuning on the real test environment, NereidVLA achieves 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials, compared with 47.50% for InternVLA-N1. Cameron Mehlman, Arjun Mulchandani, Hovik Grigoryan, Anurag Koyyada, Gregory Falco
A team of skilled card players share no information amongst each other, and yet still are able to coordinate their play by watching the same players and reading the same tells. Autonomous systems have failed to exploit this logic, relying instead on explicit communication or complex state estimation schemes that can fail when it matters most. Without it, decentralized agents diverge in their world beliefs, and coordination collapses. Here we show that anchoring all agents to a single shared external actor, a common witness whose reactions encode team state, produces spontaneous, communication-free coordination. An allocentric belief network trained on witness behavior allows each agent to independently reconstruct full team state, keeping group beliefs consistent with no inter-agent exchange. Across five competitive environments allocentric belief alignment outperforms egocentric approaches in collective performance, and even scales to sixty-agent teams where standard methods fail. These results establish a new principle for collective intelligence: in the absence of communication, a shared gaze replaces a shared channel.

World models are increasingly used in autonomous driving to predict how a scene evolves under the ego vehicle's actions, supporting counterfactual reasoning and model-based planning. However, existing evaluations focus on prediction fidelity and planning performance, and rarely verify that the predictions depend on the conditioning action. In this paper, we study action dependence in action-conditioned semantic forecasting, which predicts future semantic segmentation from past segmentations and the ego action. We compare a forecaster with feature-wise and input-level action conditioning against an identical model without action input, and measure action dependence with test-time action interventions scored by standard segmentation metrics. The evaluation is validated in a synthetic environment with known action-dependent dynamics and applied to Cityscapes and BDD100K, both within each dataset and across the two vehicle platforms. Experiments show that the executed action improves mid-term mIoU by at most 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K, whereas a wrong action reduces it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, below the model without action input. On real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6 times more on the action than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy, whereas both depend on it equally in the synthetic environment, where the history does not determine the action. These results show that an accuracy gain indicates that a driving world model uses its action, but not how strongly its forecasts depend on it. Code is available at https://github.com/binayksingh/does-action-matter.

Together, these results demonstrate that human experience can support both manipulation skill acquisition and subsequent policy improvement, reducing reliance on action-labeled robot data. Videos, dataset and code are available at https://diwali.cs.uni-freiburg.de.
♻ ☆ StableGrasp: Reconstructing Physically Stable Human Hand Grasps from Single Images
Han Jiang, Georgios Pavlakos, Qixing Huang, Etienne Vouga
Reconstructing a physically stable human grasp from a single RGB image is challenging because physically modeling grasps is itself difficult, and the problem requires estimating not only a visually constrained hand pose but also a single static hand control that stabilizes the grasp. Existing methods either model only visual hand geometry without considering physics, or are evaluated with incomplete physical modeling, which limits the physical validity of the resulting grasps. In this paper, we present StableGrasp, a differentiable simulation-based optimization framework that explicitly separates the visual hand pose from a control target that determines the grasping forces. Our method jointly optimizes hand geometry and control by minimizing the kinetic energy of the grasp in a differentiable simulator, while regularizing the hand geometry to preserve visual consistency and geometric plausibility. The reconstructed grasps are substantially more stable under physical simulation with complete physical modeling, while remaining visually consistent with the input images and geometrically plausible. Experiments show that our approach produces far more stable grasps than alternative hand-control strategies, benefiting visual-only grasp reconstruction pipelines by turning their outputs into physically stable grasps.
♻ ☆ ConDR: Conservative Reachability through Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Subsolutions
Kendra Givens, Taylor T. Johnson, Bryan C. Ward, Thomas Beckers
Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) Reachability identifies the unsafe states of a dynamical system from which it can be forced into failure under worst-case disturbance. However, classical grid-based solvers scale exponentially with state dimension. DeepReach improves scalability by replacing the grid with a neural value function trained on the HJ-Isaacs (HJI) variational inequality (VI), but penalizes both sides of the residual equally. This allows the learned value to lie above the true one and unsafe states to be misclassified as safe. We propose Conservative DeepReach (ConDR) which aims to learn a subsolution of the HJI VI such that the learned unsafe set contains the true one. ConDR enforces the obstacle branch and terminal condition by construction, pushes the HJI residual to a safety margin $ε$ below zero with a one-sided loss, and prevents the degenerate solution of classifying everything as unsafe. We prove that the exact solution of the margin-shifted VI that ConDR trains toward is a subsolution of the original VI so its unsafe set contains the true one and its value lies within $ετ$ of the true value function. We compare against DeepReach and MADR in the established systems of Air3D, Air6D, a 9D multi-vehicle system, and a 13D quadrotor. ConDR reports the lowest rate of unsafe state misclassified and the lowest closed-loop collision rates with at most a small increase in intervention. On Air3D and Air6D, ConDR tolerates model mismatch that scales with $ε$. At matched false-negative rates, ConDR's unsafe sets are smaller than the baselines showing the safety is not obtained by trivial over-approximation.

Hangong Chen, Linfeng Cheng, Tahsin Zaman Jilan, Jiaye Wu, Lee Caesar, Ian Fuller Yantian Zha
We present Video2SwimFish, an automated pipeline and benchmark for building controllable fish assets from real-fish videos for underwater embodied AI. Given synchronized multi-view videos of an individual fish, the pipeline generates a metrically scaled deformable mesh from a VLM-selected canonical frame, builds internal articulation adapted to that individual's morphology through a VLM actor-critic loop, and extracts a Biological Locomotion Manifold (BLM). The BLM provides a low-dimensional action space bounded by real-fish motion. Compared with learning directly in joint space, it lets the individual swimming policy of each reconstructed fish converge faster and reach a higher task success rate. We release two paired datasets: synchronized top- and front-view recordings of 120 individual fish across 6 species, and the controllable assets and individual swimming policies derived from them. Because every asset is tied to the animal it came from, the dataset supports a benchmark that evaluates locomotion learning not only on task success but on fidelity to that individual's locomotion behavior. We evaluate on two tasks, 3D trajectory following and target reaching, and a case study in which a simulated BlueROV underwater robot captures the assets. We further validate biological realism with a human study in which fish experts rate the simulated fish, as a complement to the automated metrics. We find that task success and locomotion fidelity do not necessarily improve together, and we identify faithful reproduction of individual animal locomotion as an open challenge for the community. Sequential manipulation in clutter requires selecting which objects to remove and determining how to manipulate them. Learning both decisions jointly can complicate training and make failures difficult to diagnose. We present Unveiler, a modular framework that separates scene reasoning and object selection from action execution through a discrete object-index interface. Its Spatial Relationship Encoder (SRE) selects the best object to grasp, while a separate Action Decoder generates orientation-discretized push-grasp actions. The SRE is trained in two stages: imitation learning from heuristic demonstrations, followed by search-based policy improvement using simulated object removals. This training procedure requires no real-robot training data and allows the SRE to be paired with a different execution policy. We evaluate Unveiler in PyBullet simulation and on a physical Dofbot-Pro. In real-robot experiments, it retrieves two occluded targets in the prescribed order in 90\% of scenes, compared with 20-30\% for the heuristic, GPT-4o, and the imitation-only variant. In PyBullet, Unveiler achieves the highest task-completion rate across all six clutter-density and occlusion conditions, reaching 90.0\% under full occlusion with 6-9 objects, compared with 67.5\% for the heuristic and 60.0\% for ThinkGrasp. These results demonstrate the potential of modular, object-centric spatial reasoning for sequential manipulation in clutter.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first integrated biomimetic robotic system, combining novel hardware, control, and field experiments, deployed to autonomously follow real marine animals. With all perception and control running onboard, the robot can hold a commanded depth, navigate around obstacles (91% success rate in the aquarium exhibit with complex lighting and visual features including glass panels) and successfully identify and follow sea turtles fully autonomously. Cheryl Wang, Chun Kwang Tan, Balint K. Athletic performance represents the pinnacle of human motor intelligence, demanding rapid choices, precise control, agility, and coordinated physical execution. Replicating this seamless combination of capabilities remains elusive in current artificial intelligence and robotic systems. Concurrently, understanding the biological mastery of these movements is hindered because complex muscle coordination is rarely measured in vivo due to the limitations of physical equipment. To bridge this fundamental gap in understanding, MyoChallenge at NeurIPS 2025 established a pioneering benchmark for motor control intelligence in sports, leveraging high-fidelity musculoskeletal models within physics simulation combined with machine learning-driven algorithms. Marking the fourth iteration of the MyoChallenge series, this event attracted almost 70 teams and over 560 submissions globally, uniting a diverse community ranging from physicians and neuroscientists to machine learning experts. The competition facilitated the development of several state-of-the-art control algorithms for a musculoskeletal system capable of sports agility, leveraging techniques such as physics-based motion planners, on-policy behaviour cloning, hierarchical planning, and muscle synergies. In this paper, we propose a novel friction model based on complementarity constraints under the Coulomb friction assumption. This model predicts various friction effects caused by environmental interactions, including both static and sliding frictions and hysteresis behavior, as well as the corresponding robot deformation induced by these interactions, which are crucial for the practical motion planning and control of continuum robots. Additionally, real-time implementation of this model can be achieved, meeting the demand for computational efficiency in robotic applications. This leads to brittle action policies that ignore language instructions in favor of visual shortcuts, despite the base VLM having this knowledge, which is a failure mode we term instruction blindness. We hypothesize that standard finetuning with limited data applies gradients to a sparse set of points, which manifests as a sharp loss landscape with high-curvature minima. We analyze this effect, then show that regularization through explicit flatness-preserving optimization is a simple yet effective technique while finetuning on the exact same data. Specifically, we demonstrate that applying sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) during VLA finetuning significantly improves instruction following by over 55% across multiple simulation and real-world benchmarks without additional data, architectural modification, or pretraining. We further analyze the effect of selective sharpness, quantify its effects, and show that such approaches are complementary to existing guidance techniques.

Neural state-space identification learns dynamical models from measured inputs and outputs. SUBNET combines this task with an encoder that estimates initial states from short measurement histories. Its continuous-time version requires many successive neural-network evaluations during numerical integration, resulting in slow training speed which is a major limitation for practical use cases. Custom GPU kernels implemented with Triton reduce the launch and memory overhead of their sequential evaluation. We explain this construction, describe a port-Hamiltonian variant, and present various benchmark comparisons of accuracy and training time.

Current records are based on sophisticated, exhaustive searches, with optimality proven only for instances up to dimension 8, motivating our study of IP formulations. We address symmetries and potential strengthenings. With the smallest open instance having as few as 512 binary decision variables, the proposed IPs offer a challenging and intriguing combinatorial problem. In addition, we extend the problem to higher-dimensional grid graphs and provide solutions for unexplored and unsolved instances.

Rather than invoking averaging theorems, we work directly with the exact dynamics of the parameter estimation error. In the scalar setting, the demodulated gradient has an explicit sinusoidal structure, which is exploited through a change of variables that absorbs the zero-mean oscillatory perturbation, together with a quadratic Lyapunov function and the persistence of excitation of the probing signal. For a sufficiently fast dither, the estimation error is shown to decay exponentially to a residual neighborhood of the origin whose size is quantified by the dither amplitude and frequency, and by the relative threshold and the offset of the event generator. All constants, including the input-to-state stability gain of the extremum seeking loop, the admissible dither frequency and the positive lower bound on the time between two consecutive events, are given in closed form, so that Zeno behavior is excluded. Compared with the trivial enumerative construction, the proposed method reduces the worst-case product-term count from linear to logarithmic in the representable range. Except at one non-vacuous boundary threshold for each bound, it also reduces both product-term count and degree. The resulting single-bound penalties have minimum positive value 1 and maximum value at most the bit width, which may simplify penalty-weight selection. On the appearance of an object, the decision maker must decide whether to accept that object (and thus stop searching) or irrevocably reject it (and thus continue searching). Simulations on grid and Barabasi-Albert networks show that, unlike the standard equal and residual-capacity redistribution approaches, the proposed method prevents secondary failures in all tested cases, with a tradeoff against served load on scale-free networks.

On the 115 cases successfully solved by all three methods, our method takes roughly half the time of either baseline, measured by geometric-mean solve time.

☆ Action-Dependent Policies for Multi-Agent Linear Quadratic Regulation
Yongjie Liu, Gangshan Jing, Long Wang
The linear quadratic regulation (LQR) problem over a multi-agent system usually requires a distributed feedback gain that is structurally constrained by the network topology, incurring an inevitable suboptimality gap. Existing studies either identify conditions on the system and topology that enable convex relaxation or seek a stationary point via policy gradient algorithms. In this paper, we reduce the suboptimality gap by adopting action-dependent policies (ADPs), where the control input of each agent depends on not only states of neighbor agents, but also control inputs of some other agents. We show that although exhibiting a distributed structure, ADP can enlarge the feasible set of feedback gains and even represent centralized optimal policies under suitable conditions. However, this comes at the price of losing coercivity of the cost function and possible failure of convergence for the projected gradient flow (PGF). To overcome this difficulty, we propose a partially regularized formulation, which guarantees convergence of PGFs, and forges a connection between standard multi-agent LQR and its action-dependent counterpart. Sufficient conditions for local convergence to globally optimal policies under PGFs regardless of regularization are also established. Finally, numerical examples are presented to validate the performance of ADP.

Our result is achieved by replacing the linearization technique in an earlier work of Leng et al. (arXiv:2504.14841), which establishes a similar subexponential quantum speedup using a transverse field Ising mixer rather than $-\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$.

These methods require the use of Newton's method to solve a moderately sized system of nonlinear equations with a dense Jacobian, the computation of which grows cubically with the number of stages, that is, the number of abscissa. To mitigate this we investigate the use of the family of Diagonally Implicit Runge-Kutta (DIRK) methods whose Butcher tableaux are lower triangular. We describe the structure exploiting linear algebra required to make the DIRK methods competitive with fully implicit methods, including efficient sensitivity calculations. Finally, we evaluate the performance of DIRK methods on several example systems, and show that the efficient implementation yields Pareto optimal integration schemes. The Linear Complementarity Problem (LCP) is a fundamental mathematical model arising in optimization, equilibrium theory, and various scientific and engineering applications. Its complementarity structure admits several equivalent mathematical representations, which provide a foundation for developing a wide range of iterative solution methods. This review presents a systematic and critical analysis of the principal reformulations of the LCP, with particular emphasis on minimum-function, projection-based, positive-negative part, and modulus-based formulations. The mathematical equivalence of these representations to the standard LCP is examined, highlighting their underlying relationships and the preservation of the complementarity conditions. Building upon these formulations, the review surveys the corresponding iterative methods developed in the existing literature, focusing on their mathematical foundations, algorithmic structures, and convergence requirements. A comparative perspective is developed to discuss the relative advantages and limitations of the different approaches, emphasizing that the suitability of an iterative method depends on the structural properties of the underlying LCP and the specific algorithm employed. In addition, relevant performance measures, including iteration count, CPU time, complementarity residual, memory requirements, and parameter sensitivity, are discussed as criteria for numerical evaluation. Finally, the review identifies important challenges and potential research directions, particularly in adaptive parameter selection, effective matrix-splitting strategies, scalable implementations, and reproducible numerical benchmarking, with the aim of supporting the development of reliable and computationally efficient methods for solving LCPs

Zhouxing Luo, Lei Wang, Xin Liu
Principal component analysis (PCA) is a fundamental and ubiquitous technique for dimension reduction and representation learning, yet its empirical formulation remains vulnerable to distributional uncertainty. While distributionally robust optimization (DRO) offers a natural remedy, existing order-2 Wasserstein models of PCA either preserve the nominal PCA subspace or lack an exact reformulation. This paper demonstrates how the infinity-Wasserstein distance can reconcile these two desirable properties. For the resulting DRO model of PCA, we derive an exact finite-dimensional reformulation and explicitly identify a worst-case distribution attaining the inner maximum. Crucially, the reformulated objective retains samplewise residual information beyond the empirical covariance matrix, revealing a mechanism through which distributional robustness can reshape the learned principal subspace. Under the mild assumption that the true distribution has a finite fourth moment, we further establish a uniform finite-sample performance guarantee for the proposed model. An iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization algorithm is also developed to solve the resulting nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization problem, with a rigorous analysis of its convergence properties. Numerical experiments substantiate the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm and the practical effectiveness of the infinity-Wasserstein model in downstream applications.

Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.

This paper addresses this gap by embedding a high-fidelity AIDC model, with separate inference and training pools, hall thermal mass, PV, a battery energy storage system (BESS) with reactive capability, and a STATCOM, in a five-minute multi-period AC optimal power flow. Simulations on the RTS-GMLC test system show that active-power flexibility mitigates local price spikes and relieves congestion, whereas reactive support from the BESS inverter or a STATCOM is needed to keep the POI voltage away from sagging around its 0.95~pu limit. Sensitivity analyses show that cost-driven charging of large batteries can induce new morning congestion and that storage largely substitutes for wider workload deferral.

Short-term scheduling in multi-product mineral manufacturing requires coordinating material movement and production across interconnected processing stages while addressing confirmed customer orders and longer-term production requirements. This work develops a generalized network-based, lexicographic multi-objective optimization (MOO) scheduling framework for these systems. The formulation represents the progression of material from raw-material supply through production and inventory to customer fulfillment. A sequential objective hierarchy first prioritizes fulfillment of confirmed customer orders and then progressively directs feasible production capacity toward cumulative targets supplied by the facility's demand-planning process. This approach ensures that the performance achieved for each higher-priority objective is preserved before subsequent targets are considered. Selected product-line activation decisions are represented using generalized disjunctive programming (GDP). An industrial mineral-manufacturing case study demonstrates the proposed framework's ability to generate feasible shift-level schedules and preserve the intended operational priorities with practical computational performance.

Existing work reveals a computational--statistical trade-off: the sketching solver (and its accelerated variants) reduces the per-step cost of Newton methods from $O(d^3)$ to $O(d^2)$, but the randomness introduced by sketching also inflates the limiting covariance of both the last and the averaged Newton iterates. In this work, we address this trade-off via gradient averaging. We show that simply replacing the stochastic gradient with a moving average at each step can mitigate, and in some cases eliminate, the trade-off in Newton sketch. Importantly, gradient averaging requires no additional oracle evaluations and leaves the contraction bound of the inner sketching solver unchanged. In particular, we prove that the last sketched Newton iterate with gradient averaging attains a limiting covariance no larger than that without gradient averaging, while the averaged iterate even attains the minimax optimal limiting covariance, matching that of the exact Newton method. To our knowledge, this is the first analysis showing that randomness introduced to improve computational efficiency need not compromise statistical efficiency as long as proper gradient estimates are used. The key analytical challenge is that gradient averaging destroys the crucial martingale difference structure underlying central limit theorem arguments. We overcome this challenge by analyzing the coupled two-timescale recursions governing the iterate and the gradient estimator. Numerical experiments on linear and logistic regression support our theoretical covariance comparisons.

We then derive theorems of the alternative that provide SOS certificates for infeasibility of systems of strict inequalities involving Jensen-type polynomials and universally quantified variables. We illustrate our results through two applications, with numerical examples. First, we show that source-localization problems admit an exact SOS reformulation under a simple dimension condition, and that an optimal solution can be recovered by solving a semidefinite program (SDP) and applying the explicit Jensen map. Second, our SOS certificates yield two {\it convergent} SDP hierarchies for semi-infinite optimization with Jensen-type polynomials, providing upper and lower bounds on the optimal value. ☆ Statistical robustness and time consistency in risk averse optimization
Alexander Shapiro, Yan Li
The aim of this manuscript is to investigate risk measures which are not necessarily convex. We show that law invariant coherent risk measures are not robust with respect to contamination of the probability measure, in the sense that an arbitrarily small contamination can change their values by an arbitrary amount. This contrasts with the Value-at-Risk, which is robust against such contamination. In addition, we show that for a given law invariant risk measure and a given policy, one can construct, under mild conditions, conditional risk measures with respect to which this policy is time consistent, in the frameworks of both Markov Decision Processes and Stochastic Optimal Control.

We focus on the practically important setting in which direct sampling from the conditional distribution of $Y \mid X$ is infeasible, and only a stream of i.i.d. observation pairs $\{(X^k, Y^k)\}_{k=0,1,2,\ldots}$ is available. Using a specially designed measure of non-optimality, combining the squared norm of the objective function's gradient and the mean square error of the auxiliary parametric model, we establish that the method achieves a convergence rate of order $\mathcal{O}\big(1/\sqrt{N}\big)$, where $N$ denotes the number of observed pairs. We develop the first active learning method for contextual linear optimization. Specifically, we introduce a label acquisition algorithm that sequentially decides whether to request the ``labels'' of feature samples arriving in an unlabeled data stream, where the labels correspond to the objective coefficients in the linear optimization problem. The label acquisition rule is guided by the decision loss induced by the predicted coefficients, known as the Smart Predict-then-Optimize (SPO) loss. The algorithm processes incoming feature samples in batches, acquiring within each batch only the labels of samples whose distance to degeneracy falls below a rejection threshold. These bounds demonstrate that, under certain natural conditions, our margin-based active learning algorithm requires fewer labels than supervised learning to achieve the same excess population risk for the chosen training loss. We provide concrete examples in which these conditions hold under continuous (sub-)Gaussian noise. Finally, we present numerical evidence demonstrating the practical value of our approach in applications such as personalized pricing and shortest-path problems.

In this paper, we propose an accelerated multiobjective gradient flow with implicit Hessian-driven damping for unconstrained convex multiobjective optimization problems in a real Hilbert space. The continuous flow is formulated as a system of two first-order equations involving only a single multiobjective projection operator and suitable time-scaling factors. Formally, it can also be expressed as a second-order system with explicit multiobjective Hessian-driven damping, which corresponds to the usual Hessian-driven damping introduced by Alvarez et al. [J. Math. Pures Appl., 81(8):747--779, 2002]. The first-order formulation, however, involves no Hessian term and can be regarded as an extension of the Hessian-driven Nesterov accelerated gradient flow by Chen and Luo [arXiv:1912.09276, 2019]. Assuming that the objective gradients are Lipschitz continuous on bounded sets and that the common lower level sets are bounded, we establish global existence in finite dimensions under suitable time-scaling conditions. An a priori energy estimate confines the solutions to a fixed bounded set, and a Lyapunov argument yields fast decay of a merit function and the KKT residual. Under an additional bound on the time-scaling factors, the trajectory of every global solution converges weakly to a weak Pareto point. Numerical tests illustrate the rapid residual decay and reduced oscillations.
♻ ☆ When Does Reallocating a Sampling Budget Pay? Instance-wise Allocation for Neural Routing Solvers
Jinhyung Bae
Neural routing solvers sample many solutions per instance and keep the best, with the same number of samples for every instance. We measure how much a non-uniform split of the same total budget is worth and which property of a workload decides it. Best-of-k curves estimated by averaging random orderings of stored samples overstate the gain, and deciding on one half of the samples while evaluating on the other understates it; we use exact best-of-k curves, a U-statistic over all orderings. For three pretrained solvers (POMO, the Attention Model and Sym-NCO) on the traveling salesman problem, reallocation reduces the total optimality gap by at most 2.5% on the training distribution, so uniform allocation is close to optimal there. On workloads that mix in out-of-distribution instances it reduces the gap by 11.8-13.3% (1.1-1.8% of tour length) for the two solvers that degrade under the shift, and almost nothing for the one that does not. Across two heterogeneity mechanisms, three solvers, two confirmation collections and budgets of 25 to 200 samples per instance, the gain is predicted by the spread of difficulty within a workload, not its average. Allocating on a power-law curve fitted to twenty charged probe samples per instance recovers 88-93% of the uncharged optimum; successive halving does worse. Consensus-based optimization (CBO) is a powerful and versatile zero-order multi-particle method designed to provably solve high-dimensional global optimization problems, including those that are genuinely nonconvex or nonsmooth. The method relies on a balance between stochastic exploration and contraction toward a consensus point, which is defined via the Laplace principle as a proxy for the global minimizer. In this paper, we introduce new CBO variants that address practical and theoretical limitations of the original formulation of this novel optimization methodology. First, we propose a model called $δ$-CBO}, which incorporates nonvanishing diffusion to prevent premature collapse to suboptimal states. We also develop a numerically stable implementation, the Consensus Freezing scheme, that remains robust even for arbitrarily large time steps by freezing the consensus point over time intervals. We connect these models through appropriate asymptotic limits. Furthermore, we derive from the Consensus Freezing scheme by suitable time rescaling and asymptotics a further algorithm, the Consensus Hopping scheme, which can be interpreted as a form of $(1,λ)$-Evolution Strategy. For all these schemes, we characterize for the first time the invariant measures and establish global convergence results, including exponential convergence rates.

In this paper, we establish that for convex absolutely continuous immersions of $S^{1}$ in the plane, the shape distance induced by the square root velocity transformation (SRVT) is indeed equivalent to the WFR distance acting on their associated length measures. The proof exploits a monotonicity principle for optimal transport on the universal cover of the circle, which in turn guarantees the existence of an optimal reparametrization achieving the SRVT infimum and enables a one-dimensional unbalanced optimal transport reformulation. Motivated by this equivalence, we further investigate the role of sparsity in shape optimization problems formulated in terms of length measures and regularized by the WFR distance. This readily yields a Poincaré inequality for $κ$-strongly log-concave sources. The coefficient $(1/κ)^{1/2}$ is shown to be optimal. The proof relies on a probabilistic interpretation of cell energies and the subsequent variance decomposition. Interpolation from potential to map then yields the map stability for targets in a common compact set, \[ \left\Vert T_μ-T_ν\right\Vert _{L^{2}(ρ)}\leqslant \operatorname{Const} \cdot W_{2}\left( μ,ν\right) ^{1/3}. \] Sharpness of the order for both the potential and map stability are established. This clarifies a long- standing limitation in topological embedding: representing distributions by their Brenier maps preserves convergence, but it need not preserve local distances.

Through the use of a finite-horizon Yosida approximation of the Koopman generator and an empirical sampling operator, the data-driven solution of the observer gain can be reduced to a finite-dimensional subspace specified by the sample and hence fulfilled by convex semidefinite programming (SDP). We study a distributionally robust chance-constrained variant whose ambiguity set is a Wasserstein ball around the sampled distribution and make four contributions. Third, our formulation is, by construction, the minimization of the worst-case Value-at-Risk of the random quadratic form; this unifies it with existing frameworks for uncertain standard quadratic optimization problems, in particular under chance constraints, and we identify natural settings in which it collapses to a single deterministic instance. Finally, we report numerical experiments on positive definite and indefinite instances which quantify how the model parameters drive the optimal value and solution time, and expose the computational cost of indefiniteness.

Both the synthetic experiments and the numerical studies on temperature sensor monitoring, sleep-stage classification, and hospital nurse staffing demonstrate the effectiveness of \texttt{DisSigUCB} over linear and kernelized contextual bandit baselines in nonlinear and path-dependent settings.

♻ ☆ A 5/2 Guarantee for Echelon Stock (s,S) Policies in One-Warehouse Multi-Retailer Systems
Ming Hu
We study a periodic-review warehouse serving multiple heterogeneous retailers with stochastic demand and fixed costs and lead times at both echelons. We construct a deterministic echelon stock (s,S) policy whose long-run expected average cost is at most 5/2 times the optimum over all nonanticipative policies. The guarantee holds when, as in a retail chain with common service penalties, the uniform backlog penalty and heterogeneous retailer holding rates are at least the warehouse holding rate and heterogeneous retailer setup costs are at most 3/2 times the supplier's. The latter setup-cost condition extends beyond supplier setup-cost dominance: a retailer dispatch may incur a setup cost up to 50 percent higher than a supplier order's. Demand vectors are i.i.d. over periods with finite positive means, and demands of different retailers may be correlated. Each retailer selects the full cycle of its single-location plan or a shifted cycle of half its width, under an inflated setup cost, and the warehouse serves requests in arrival order, allowing partial shipments. The upper bound on the policy's cost includes each retailer's mirror cost, which prices the warehouse imbalance created by that retailer's batching. The upper and lower bounds share a pooled supplier problem and add one problem per retailer, giving a factor independent of all lead times and the number of retailers. For arbitrary nonnegative setup costs and associated retailer demands, a consolidation policy holds allocated stock until a dispatch threshold is met and gives a factor below 4.9. On 864 instances built from Walmart store sales, the simulated cost of an integer-rounded implementation of the FIFO policy averages 1.45 times the lower bound and reaches 1.75, and our analytical upper bound on its cost is below 1.94 times the lower bound; both ratios to the lower bound have nearly the same mean at every supplier lead time.

♻ ☆ Finite de Finetti for convex bodies and Polynomial Optimization
Julius A. Zeiss, Gereon Koßmann, René Schwonnek, Martin Plávala
We study polynomial optimization over convex bodies with separately affine objectives and local affine equality and inequality constraints. We construct a convergent hierarchy of conic relaxations with explicit finite-level error bounds of order $n^{-1/2}$ at level $n$, complemented by a constructive rounding scheme that produces feasible points. The relaxation bounds and rounded objective values bracket the optimum at the same rate. The analytic ingredient is a finite de Finetti representation theorem for arbitrary proper cones: bipartite marginals of symmetric extensions in maximal tensor products are $O(n^{-1/2})$-close, in base norm, to points of the minimal tensor product. Its proof combines a uniform, monogamy-type bound on a variational mutual information based on Frenkel's relative entropy with classical conditioning and informationally complete measurements. We apply the framework to the assemblage relaxation of two-player non-local games in general probabilistic theories. For polytopic state spaces, the hierarchy consists of linear programs, and experiments on the Clauser--Horne--Shimony--Holt (CHSH) game provide a numerical proof of concept for the outer approximations and feasible rounding procedure.

♻ ☆ Coupled Stochastic Multigrid Reconstruction for Blind Ptychography
Borong Zhang, Junjing Deng, Yi Jiang, Zichao Wendy Di
Blind ptychography enables quantitative imaging when both the specimen and illumination probe are unknown, but modern data sets call for reconstruction methods that can assimilate many diffraction patterns while resolving structure across spatial scales. We introduce a coupled stochastic multigrid framework that addresses these requirements within a unified optimization construction. Rather than appending multigrid correction to an existing stochastic algorithm, the framework begins with a common surrogate for the local object and probe updates and connects these updates to minibatch consensus and coarse-grid correction through a unified residual analysis. This analysis establishes local control of the geometric-mean coupling and characterizes its extension across a grid hierarchy. The fine-grid construction yields the geometric-mean regularized Ptychographical Iterative Engine (GM-rPIE), while the inclusion of multilevel corrections yields the geometric-mean Multilevel-Adaptive-Guided Ptychographic Iterative Engine (GM-MAGPIE). Across nine synthetic configurations spanning scan overlap and Poisson noise, GM-MAGPIE achieves the lowest final object error at the prescribed budgets, while either GM-rPIE or GM-MAGPIE achieves the lowest probe error. Reconstructions of experimental test-pattern and integrated-circuit data further demonstrate the framework's applicability to measured X-ray data.

♻ ☆ Efficient Hessian-Free Methods for Multi-Objective Bilevel Optimization with a Nonconvex Lower-Level Objective
Yicong Jiang, Feihu Huang
Multi-objective bilevel optimization has wide applications in the AI area such as automated learning and multi-task meta-learning. Although some recent studies have investigated multi-objective bilevel optimization, many existing methods rely on the (strongly) convex lower level problems. In fact, these multi-objective bilevel learning problems are generally nonconvex, and particularly their lower level problems are nonconvex. To fill this gap, we propose a class of Multi-Objective Moreau Envelope based Hessian-free Algorithms (MOMEHA) for the multi-objective bilevel learning problems with a nonconvex lower level. Specifically, our method uses the Moreau envelope to formulate a multi-objective single-level relaxation that enforces lower-level first-order stationarity. In particular, our method retains computational advantages of being single-loop and Hessian-free in the multi-objective setting by incorporating a smooth weighted Tchebycheff scalarization. Furthermore, we propose a momentum variant of MOMEHA (i.e., MB-MOMEHA) for the stochastic multi-objective bilevel learning problems. Under the stated assumptions, we establish finite-iteration bounds on the Moreau gap and Pareto stationarity residuals under dynamically relaxed gap constraints in both deterministic and stochastic settings. Some experiments on few-shot meta-learning and neural architecture search demonstrate that our methods outperform the existing approaches in terms of Pareto front quality, validating their effectiveness and robustness.

♻ ☆ Dynamic Programming for Indefinite Stochastic McKean-Vlasov LQ Control Problem under Input Constraints
Xun Li, Liangquan Zhang
In this note, we study a class of indefinite stochastic McKean-Vlasov linear-quadratic (LQ in short) control problem under the control taking nonnegative values. In contrast to the conventional issue, both the classical dynamic programming principle (DPP in short) and the usual Riccati equation approach fail. We tackle these difficulties by extending the state space from $\mathbb{R}$ to probability measure space, afterward derive the the corresponding the infinite dimensional Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB in short) equation. The optimal control and value function can be obtained basing on two functions constructed via two groups of novelty ordinary differential equations satisfying the HJB equation mentioned before. As an application, we revisit the mean-variance portfolio selection problems in continuous time under the constraint that short-selling of stocks is prohibited. The investment risk and the capital market line can be captured simultaneously.
♻ ☆ A Unified Theory of Solvability for Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Control Problems I: The Homogeneous Case
Hongwei Mei
The existing theory of stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problems focuses on open-loop and closed-loop solvability. For finite horizon problems, it is widely accepted that those two types of solvability are not equivalent in general, as demonstrated by explicit counterexamples. In contrast, they coincide in standard infinite-horizon formulations with constant coefficients under suitable stabilizability and integrability assumptions. This paper aims at challenging this well-established paradigm by developing a novel framework of closed-loop solvability, namely generalized closed-loop solvability, which removes the $L^2$-integrability constraint on the feedback strategies from the existing formulation. It will be proven that open-loop and generalized closed-loop solvability are equivalent and the classical closed-loop solvablity is a particular case only when the admissible feedback strategy is $L^2$-integrable over the time horizon. In other words, the previously established non-equivalence between open-loop and closed-loop solvability stems solely from the limitations of the classical formulation which requires the $L^2$-integrability of the admissible feedback strategies over the time-horizon. Therefore, this paper unifies the theory of the solvabilitiy for stochastic LQ control problems. Moreover, our results offer a novel insight to stochastic LQ control problems: open-loop/generalized closed-loop solvability is essentially equivalent to piecewisely local closed-loop solvability in the classical sense. The current paper is focused on homogeneous cases only and non-homogeneous cases will be studied in a subsequent paper.

We study variance-dependent reinforcement learning in episodic time-inhomogeneous linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with feature dimension $d$, horizon $H$, and $K$ episodes. While recent works have established variance-dependent regret with $\tilde{O}(1)$ deterministic-regime overhead for linear mixture MDPs (Zhao et al., 2023) and worst-case nearly minimax optimal regret $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K} + d^7 H^8)$ for linear MDPs (He et al., 2023),, existing variance-aware analyses for linear MDPs (Li and Sun, 2023; Huang et al., 2023) rely on a coarse concentration step whose resulting regret guarantees retain a polynomial $\tilde{O}(K^{1/4})$ additive term even in deterministic environments. We propose VA-LSVI-UCB++, a computationally efficient algorithm that achieves the variance-dependent regret bound $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H\min\{\mathrm{Var}_K^*,\mathrm{Var}_K^π\}}+d^5H^4)$, where $\mathrm{Var}_K^*$ and $\mathrm{Var}_K^π$ denote the cumulative conditional variances of the optimal value function and the played policies' value functions along the realized trajectory. Our result adapts to the minimum of the two realized trajectory variances, recovers the worst-case minimax optimal leading term $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K})$, and collapses to $\tilde{O}(d^5 H^4)$ in deterministic environments, free of polynomial-in-$K$ dependency. At the core of our analysis is a simultaneous three-way reference-advantage decomposition for the optimistic, pessimistic, and squared value function estimators coupled with variance self-bounding and Freedman-type value-difference arguments, which tightens the pessimistic and second-moment confidence radii by a factor of $\tilde{O}(d H)$ and removes the inverse-variance-floor blowup.

☆ A Feasible-Domain Reduction Approach with Objective-Loss Guarantees for Multilevel Multiobjective Linear Programming

In some approaches to decentralized multilevel multiobjective programming, each decision-maker selects a compromise and restricts the feasible region before passing the decision to the next level. However, these restrictions do not necessarily limit the deterioration of objective values at preceding levels. This paper studies how to choose variable bounds that keep such losses within prescribed tolerances. We establish exact conditions using linear programming duality and derive simpler bounds based on objective coefficients. We also examine the choice of restriction widths and establish guarantees for successive reductions. A two-level numerical example illustrates the results and the influence of tolerances on the final compromise.

An exact Rényi-2 entropy identity shows that partitioning alters both spectral concentration and graph-volume normalization, explaining why unregularized entropy minimization can favor degenerate solutions. Across a 243-condition population-analytic factor recovery benchmark, DEFI achieved an overall exact recovery rate of 97.2\% (versus 75.0\% for EGA-TMFG, 45.8\% for TEFI on von Neumann entropy). Across ten clustering benchmarks, DEFI-guided Gaussian mixtures achieved a mean ARI of 0.929, exceeding HDBSCAN (0.809), Ward clustering (0.700), and conventional GMM criteria (0.501-0.580), with gains concentrating where standard criteria over-extract components.

We develop a unified optimal-control framework that solves supervised classification and likelihood-based density estimation with a single diffeomorphic flow whose velocity lives in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS); the two tasks share all structure except the objective. Variable projection eliminates the terminal model (a classifier, or a Gaussian-mixture (GMM) reference), leaving a reduced control problem whose gradient comes from an analytic discrete adjoint. The RKHS parameterization makes the flow's divergence exact and deterministic at the cost of one kernel matrix-vector product, avoiding the stochastic trace estimators and potential-flow restrictions of existing continuous normalizing flows. Because the objective and gradient are deterministic, matrix-free reduced Gauss-Newton (GN) and related second-order solvers are practical for both tasks, which we benchmark against a range of first- and second-order optimizers; the learned map is a diffeomorphism with explicitly controlled regularity. In experiments from dimension 2 to 256, the reduced GN solvers use the fewest iterations of any optimizer tested and, together with joint L-BFGS, the least work; a multiscale kernel improves the density fit, and a trainable GMM reference reduces the deformation needed for multimodal transport at comparable likelihood while lowering the likelihood on real data. The full-model solve is quadratic in the particle count and sub-linear in dimension; a control-point reduction makes the particle-count scaling linear at near-lossless accuracy.

☆ A Graph-Theoretic Framework for Identifying Mathematical Programming Decompositions
Nicholas N. Kalamaris, Christos T. Maravelias
We develop a framework for identifying combinations of complicating variables and/or constraints that can be used to formulate mathematical programming decompositions. A mathematical program is represented by a graph which accounts for the structural and functional relationship between variables and constraints. Graph projections are used to focus on variable- or constraint-based decompositions. A series of coarsening operations is used to generate a reduced graph based on the original or projected graph. On the reduced graph, we use integer programming to identify different combinations of complicating variables and/or constraints. Specifically, variables and constraints are identified as complicating based on their structural role and/or their functionality (contribution to nonlinearity) in the mathematical program. The framework allows us to assess the viability of different decomposition types (variable, constraint, cross) and identify multiple potential decomposition formulations of the same type (e.g. different combinations of complicating variables for Benders decomposition). The systematic nature of our framework facilitates broader studies into the efficacy of different decompositions across a range of problems including energy markets, process design, and machine learning.
☆ Beyond Area: Perimeter Optimization in the Planar Skorokhod Embedding Problem

The planar Skorokhod embedding problem asks for a simply connected planar domain whose Brownian exit distribution has a prescribed real marginal $μ$. We investigate the minimization of conformal perimeter over the class of all such embeddings. We first establish the main existence theorem showing that whenever a finite-perimeter embedding exists, the infimum is attained (and vice versa). We derive necessary conditions for finiteness and sufficient conditions based on logarithmic integrability of the density. In particular, we demonstrate that finite area does not guarantee the existence of an embedding with finite perimeter. Although Gross's canonical embedding minimizes area, we construct an explicit family of domains for which Brownian symmetrization strictly increases perimeter, disproving its universal perimeter minimality. On the positive side, using Pruss's containment theorem and inequalities from convex geometry, we establish a general lower bound in terms of the convex hull of the Gross domain. Consequently, whenever the Gross embedding is bounded and convex, it is the unique perimeter minimizer. Finally, we formulate an open problem concerning the relationship between the existence of finite-perimeter embeddings and the regularity of Gross's canonical embedding.

Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $ε$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $ε$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $ε$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization. It achieves a significantly lower gradient evaluation complexity with respect to the objective function compared to existing methods, and can outperform them when computing constraint gradients and projections onto the associated cone is cheaper than evaluating the objective gradient. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.

The cost combines tracking terms, a quadratic control cost and an $L^1$ term promoting sparsity in time. We prove existence, derive optimality conditions, and show that optimal controls are thresholded functions of a switching function whose derivative is governed by the commutator of the drift and control operators.
