♻ ☆ When Should a Human Take Back Control? Optimal Delegation under Turbulent AI Risk
Haoze Yan, Julien Roze, Ved Upadhyay, Unal Tatar, Thibaut Mastrolia
When should a human take control from an autonomous AI agent, how much checking is worthwhile, and when should autonomy resume? These decisions become harder when incidents cluster and recent errors signal elevated risk. Exploratory analyses of AgentLogs coding-agent traces and ODCV-Bench task runs show higher held-out log likelihood for Hawkes incident-history models than matched no-history baselines, with positive gains whose conditional $90\%$ intervals exclude zero. AgentLogs evaluates continuous-time incident timing and type; ODCV evaluates failure occurrence at discrete decisions. Motivated by this predictive evidence, we formulate a continuous-time delegation problem that jointly chooses productive action, verification effort, and switching rates between human-directed, AI-assisted operation and autonomous AI operation. The model assumes that verification weakens incident propagation and balances project benefits against operating, supervision, risk, and handoff costs. Our Hawkes-PPO method summarizes observed incidents with exponential memory filters and learns these decisions from rewards. In synthetic experiments, it achieves a higher evaluated objective than either fixed regime and PPO without history filters, and approaches an approximate full-information benchmark. Further experiments show how incident excitation and supervision costs shape delegation.
♻ ☆ Solving Linear and Integer Programs Faster Using Data NeurIPS 2026
Yuhan Ye, Omar Bennouna
We study how much a linear program (LP) or an integer program (IP) can be compressed when solved repeatedly over a fixed feasible region with varying objective coefficients. We provide a framework that compresses LP and IP formulations with guarantees on the probability of preserving optimality, using either an uncertainty set for the cost vector or historical samples. Our framework exposes a tunable tradeoff between compression and the probability of recovering an optimal solution. We characterize the minimum dimension of affine reformulations preserving the full optimizer set over a given cost region and provide sample-based learning algorithms with fast-rate guarantees, without requiring a nondegeneracy assumption for LPs. With high confidence over the training data, the learned reformulation preserves the optimizer set for an independent test cost with probability at least $1-ρ-\widetilde{O}(d^\star_ρ/n)$, where $ρ$ bounds the excluded probability mass and $d^\star_ρ$ is the retained region's decision-relevant dimension. Existing data-driven approaches to LP and IP reduction do not, to our knowledge, learn a single low-dimensional affine reformulation with a prescribed probability of preserving the full optimizer set. Experimental results show substantial improvements over the compared baselines in accuracy, sample efficiency, and computational speed.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 32 pages, 11 figures
♻ ☆ Faster Algorithms for Structured Linear and Kernel Support Vector Machines ICLR 2025
Yuzhou Gu, Zhao Song, Lichen Zhang
Many machine learning problems are quadratic programs, including Support Vector Machines (SVMs). A general quadratic program has input size $Θ(n^2)$, and assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), no $O(n^{2-o(1)})$ time algorithm exists when the objective matrix is positive semidefinite (Backurs, Indyk, and Schmidt, NeurIPS'17). SVMs, however, are given by $n$ data points of dimension $d$, often much smaller than $n$, and have only $O(1)$ equality constraints. In this work, we design the first nearly-linear time algorithm for solving quadratic programs whenever a low-rank factorization of the quadratic objective matrix is given, the number of linear constraints is small, the coefficients of the objective and some optimal solution are bounded by $\mathrm{poly}(n)$, and some feasible point has all entries between $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ and $\mathrm{poly}(n)$. For linear SVM on $d$-dimensional data, our randomized algorithm runs in expected time $\widetilde O(nd^{(ω+1)/2}\log(n/ε))$ when $(d+1)^{ω-1}\le n$ and the data points have norms at most $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ and margin at least $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$, where $ω<2.258$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. Its output satisfies the equality constraint only approximately. For Gaussian kernel SVM, when $d=O(\log n)$, the squared dataset radius is $o(\log n/\log\log n)$ and the dual variables lie in a box $[0,R]^n$ with $R\le\mathrm{poly}(n)$, our randomized algorithm runs in expected time $n^{1+o(1)}$ for any accuracy $ε\ge 1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$. We also prove that, assuming SETH, when the squared dataset radius is $Ω(\log^2 n)$, $Ω(n^{2-o(1)})$ time is required on some inputs to reach error $\exp(-Θ(\log^2 n))$ for the program without the bias term. This improves upon the prior best lower bound in both the dimension $d$ and the squared dataset radius.

♻ ☆ Data-Driven Exploration for a Class of Continuous-Time Indefinite Linear--Quadratic Reinforcement Learning Problems
Yilie Huang, Xun Yu Zhou
We study reinforcement learning (RL) for a class of continuous-time stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) control problems, where volatilities depend on both states and controls while states are scalar-valued and there are no running control rewards, the last feature also leading to the so-called indefinite LQ controls. We propose a model-free, data-driven exploration mechanism that adaptively adjusts entropy regularization by the critic and policy variance by the actor. Unlike the constant or deterministic exploration schedules employed in the existing literature, which require extensive tuning for implementations and ignore learning progress during iterations, our adaptive exploratory approach boosts learning efficiency with minimal tuning. Despite its flexibility, our method achieves a sublinear regret bound that matches the best-known model-free results for this class of LQ problems, which were previously derived only with fixed exploration schedules. Numerical experiments demonstrate that adaptive explorations accelerate convergence and improve regret performance compared to the non-adaptive model-free and model-based counterparts.

♻ ☆ On Busemann subgradient methods for stochastic minimization in Hadamard spaces
Nicholas Pischke
We study the recently introduced Busemann subgradient method due to Goodwin, Lewis, López-Acedo and Nicolae, extending it to minimize the mean of a stochastic function over general Hadamard spaces. We prove a strong convergence theorem under a local compactness assumption and further prove weak convergence of the method over separable Hadamard spaces. The proof is based on a general (weak) convergence theorem for stochastic processes in Hadamard spaces which confine to a stochastic variant of quasi-Fejér monotonicity, together with a nonlinear variant of Pettis' theorem, which are of independent interest. Lastly, we provide best function value estimates as well as a strong convergence result under a strong convexity assumption, and in that latter case in particular derive explicit rates of convergence. We illustrate the practical use of the general mean minimization problem and the associated Busemann subgradient method through statistical models for phylogenetic inference via the Billera-Holmes-Vogtmann tree space.
comment: 31 pages
♻ ☆ Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning for Asset-Liability Management
Yilie Huang
This paper proposes a novel approach for Asset-Liability Management (ALM) by employing continuous-time Reinforcement Learning (RL) with a linear-quadratic (LQ) formulation that incorporates both interim and terminal objectives. We develop a model-free, policy gradient-based soft actor-critic algorithm tailored to ALM for dynamically synchronizing assets and liabilities. To ensure an effective balance between exploration and exploitation with minimal tuning, we introduce adaptive exploration for the actor and scheduled exploration for the critic. Our empirical study evaluates this approach against two enhanced traditional financial strategies, a model-based continuous-time RL method, and three state-of-the-art RL algorithms. Evaluated across 200 randomized market scenarios, our method achieves higher average rewards than all alternative strategies, with rapid initial gains and sustained superior performance. The outperformance stems not from complex neural networks or improved parameter estimation, but from directly learning the optimal ALM strategy without learning the environment.
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Updated publication information and corrected a typo in the caption of Figure 1
♻ ☆ Mean--Variance Portfolio Selection by Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning: Algorithms, Regret Analysis, and Empirical Study
Yilie Huang, Yanwei Jia, Xun Yu Zhou
We study continuous-time mean--variance portfolio selection in markets where stock prices are diffusion processes driven by observable factors that are also diffusion processes, yet the coefficients of these processes are unknown. Based on the recently developed reinforcement learning (RL) theory for diffusion processes, we present a general data-driven RL approach that learns the pre-committed investment strategy directly without attempting to learn or estimate the market coefficients. For multi-stock Black--Scholes markets without factors, we further devise an algorithm and prove its performance guarantee by deriving a sublinear regret bound in terms of the Sharpe ratio. We then carry out an extensive empirical study implementing this algorithm to compare its performance and trading characteristics, evaluated under a host of common metrics, with a large number of widely employed portfolio allocation strategies on S\&P 500 constituents. The results demonstrate that the proposed continuous-time RL strategy is consistently among the best, especially in a volatile bear market, and decisively outperforms the model-based continuous-time counterparts by significant margins.

♻ ☆ Adaptive Reparametrized Time for Score-Based Diffusion Sampling
Yilie Huang, Wenpin Tang, Xun Yu Zhou
We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where the learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard, but their fixed, ad hoc prescriptions can be suboptimal. We propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating sampling-clock speed as the control, so a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in diffusion time and a leading-order Euler error surrogate defines the allocation objective. To solve the resulting high-dimensional deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized Gaussian-policy formulation that turns schedule learning into continuous-time reinforcement learning. We prove ART-RL is equivalent to ART at optimality: the mean of the optimal Gaussian policy solves ART. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor-critic updates. Experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation show that ART-learned schedules, when plugged into existing samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improve sample quality over strong baselines at matched budgets. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalizability, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, data sets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.

☆ Near-Optimal Methods for Generalized Lipschitz Convex Optimization
Dmitry Kovalev, Grigory Malinovsky
In this paper, we consider a convex optimization problem, where the upper bound on the subgradient norm depends on the objective function. We establish a lower bound on the number of iterations required by any first-order method to find an approximate solution to the problem. Furthermore, we present two near-optimal algorithms that can match the lower bound up to logarithmic factors. The first algorithm is a projected GD with a carefully designed stepsize schedule which incorporates warm-up and decay phases. The second algorithm is scalar-stepsize clipped AdamW which extends the near-optimal guarantees to the stochastic setting, where only a noisy unbiased estimator of the subgradient is available.
☆ Soft-constrained Schrödinger bridge for generative AI: numerical algorithms and approximation guarantees
Jin Ma, Ying Tan, Renyuan Xu, Qinxin Yan
We study a soft-constrained formulation of the Schrödinger bridge problem, in which the terminal distribution constraint is relaxed into a penalty on the discrepancy between the terminal law of the controlled process and a target distribution. This leads to an unconstrained McKean--Vlasov stochastic control problem, where the interaction enters only through the terminal cost. We characterize the optimizer via a McKean--Vlasov forward-backward stochastic differential equation and establish well-posedness under very mild assumptions. We also analyze two approximation regimes relevant to data-driven computation: approximation of the target law by empirical samples, and finite-particle approximation of the McKean--Vlasov control problem. For both, we derive convergence results and error estimates. Finally, building on the well-posedness and approximation results, we investigate two neural numerical methods: one based on the forward-backward system and the other on direct control optimization. Both methods are tested on state-of-the-art generative tasks. Our results provide both an algorithmic foundation and its theoretical guarentee for soft-constrained Schrödinger bridge problems in sample-based generative modeling.
☆ Strengthening Compact Vehicle Routing Formulations through Arc-Flow Aggregation and Refinement
Julian Yarkony, Willem-Jan van Hoeve, Anthony Karahalios, Martin Karyamsetty, Soheyl Khalilpourazari, Louis-Martin Rousseau, Xiaohang Zhu
Arc-flow formulations can provide strong relaxations for mixed-integer program formulations of vehicle routing problems, but the associated networks may be prohibitively large. We study the setting in which multiple arc flow relaxations may be applied, and introduce a dual-guided aggregation and refinement framework that constructs substantially smaller arc-flow formulations while recovering the LP bound of the original networks. Dual information is used both to identify states that can be aggregated without weakening the bound and to guide node disaggregation. We show that the resulting procedure converges finitely to the arc-flow bound of the full arc-flow formulation. The framework retains the original decision variables, allowing cutting planes to be added directly in the original variable space. Moreover, it produces an explicit MILP formulation without relying on column generation or pricing to determine the arc-flow relaxation bound. We apply our approach to the vehicle routing problem with time windows for which we define two arc flow relaxations, as well as two families of cutting planes over the original variable space. Computational experiments show that strong bounds can be obtained using substantially aggregated networks. The resulting root bounds are competitive with those obtained by the branch-and-price solver RouteOpt, while retaining a formulation that can be solved directly by a general-purpose MILP solver.
comment: 47 pages. Submitted to Transportation Science
☆ Descending Everest, Part III: Oracle Complexity of Monotone Variational Inequalities with $(L_0,L_1)$-Lipschitz Operators
Mikhail Rudomanov, Ivan Fomin, Alexander V. Gasnikov, Fedor S. Stonyakin
We consider monotone variational inequalities in which the Jacobian norm of the operator $F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ is bounded by an affine function of the norm of the operator itself: $\|DF(z)\|\le L_0+L_1\|F(z)\|$. The main case is the problem on the whole space, that is, finding a zero of $F$. We assume that a solution exists and that an upper bound $R$ on the distance from the starting point to the solution is known. Neither strong monotonicity nor cocoercivity is assumed. Global Lipschitz continuity is not assumed either: for $L_1>0$, the Jacobian norm may grow together with the norm of the operator. We obtain upper and lower bounds on the number of oracle calls sufficient to find a point $\hat z$ with $\|F(\hat z)\|\le\varepsilon$. For $L_0R/\varepsilon\ge1$, both bounds are, up to logarithmic factors in $L_1R$, of order $1+L_0R/\varepsilon+(L_1R)^{6/5}$. The upper bound is attained by a deterministic extragradient-type method, and the lower bound holds for arbitrary randomized methods. The same bounds are obtained for the Minty gap on the ball of radius $R$, where $L_0R/\varepsilon$ is replaced by $L_0R^2/η$. In addition, we show that for a variational inequality on a bounded set the numbers $L_0,L_1$ and the diameter of the set are not sufficient: a uniform complexity bound requires additional information, for example, an upper bound on the norm of the operator at the solution.
comment: 38 pages, 2 algorithms, 1 table. Third paper in the Descending Everest series; Part I: arXiv:2610.21461, Part II: arXiv:2611.04171. A Russian version of the paper is available at https://github.com/chitoraphelion/descending-everest-with-first-order-oracles
☆ A Differential Theory of Quality-Resource Trade-offs for AI Model Selection: The Multiresource Frontier and Its Minimax Price
Dmitry Ignatov
Comparing AI models across resource budgets yields quality-resource frontiers relating error to latency, parameter count, training compute, and energy. Offset power laws summarize such frontiers, but their fitted parameters reveal neither the price-independent geometry nor the manner in which trade-offs extend across several resource channels. This paper addresses both gaps by developing a differential theory in which this structure is made explicit. Each frontier admits a price-independent plane-curve representation relating the effective number of active resource channels, $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = s^2/κ$ (squared slope over curvature), to the remaining log-error depth, $ΔS = \ln(\varepsilon/\varepsilon_{\infty})$. This representation separates intrinsic shape from the scale and origin of the resource axis. Complete monotonicity and divisibility yield differential inequalities and frontier bounds. When each of $N$ resources contributes one active channel, the theory gives the parameter-free operating rule $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1$ in delivered units and derives minimax resource prices $λ^{\star}_i = α_i/(N+1)$ with an exact worst-case regret of $\ln(N+1)$ nats. The results make it possible to interpret measured frontiers and compare resource costs without hand-chosen exchange rates. The theory is evaluated on 117 published frontiers and implemented in the open-source package nn-rank, which derives prices from measured quality and cost, ranks candidates, and reports supported choices and minimax regret: https://github.com/ABrain-One/nn-rank
comment: Under review
☆ Continuous-Time Stochastic Contraction Induced by Common White Noise
Sunghyun Koo, Jin Gyu Lee, Hyungbo Shim
This paper studies contraction properties of stochastic dynamical systems governed by Itô stochastic differential equations. We consider two trajectories driven by a common noise process and measure their separation using Finsler distances, which encompass Riemannian and norm-induced distances. Two notions of contraction are then investigated: $L^p$-contraction, defined by exponential decay of the $L^p$-norm (or the $p$-th moment) of the distance, and almost sure contraction, defined by exponential decay of the distance along almost every sample path. Each notion is characterized by a differential condition that is necessary and sufficient for contraction under mild hypotheses. Relations between contraction notions and an associated incremental input-to-state stability result are also established. As an illustration, we apply the established theory to analyze noise-induced synchronization and quantify its robustness with respect to parameter perturbations.
☆ Contraction Analysis and Control of Polynomial Dynamical Systems
Xin Mao, Anqi Dong, Can Chen
Contraction analysis has found broad applications in synchronization, tracking, observer design, and nonlinear feedback control. However, establishing contraction conditions for polynomial dynamical systems remains challenging due to their state-dependent Jacobians. In this article, we develop a tensor-based framework for contraction analysis of polynomial dynamical systems by exploiting the structure of orthogonally decomposable (odeco) coefficient tensors. By transforming the dynamics into modal coordinates, we derive necessary and sufficient semicontraction conditions and characterize state-dependent semimetrics. We establish fundamental limitations on exponential contraction and prove polynomial decay of differential displacements on forward-invariant regions. To accommodate more general polynomial dynamical systems, we extend the framework to include linear dynamics and non-odeco tensor perturbations, deriving computationally tractable contraction certificates with explicit robustness guarantees. We further develop convex feedback synthesis conditions based on linear matrix inequalities for general input matrices. We demonstrate the effectiveness and computational scalability of the proposed framework through numerical experiments on both synthetic systems and nonlinear elastic relaxation models.
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures
☆ Feasibility certificates for DeePC: A set invariance approach
Daniel O'Neill, Ross Drummond, Pablo R. Baldivieso-Monasterios
DeePC is posed on a window of past inputs and outputs, so its feasible set is a set of histories and is not available in closed form. We write the DeePC solution as an implicit ReLU network whose weights are built from Hankel matrices and whose activation patterns are the critical regions of the underlying quadratic program. This gives, directly from the Hankel matrices, the feasible set of DeePC as a polyhedral projection, its explicit piecewise-affine control law, and an exact linear model of the history window. We compute three invariant sets of histories: the maximal positively invariant set of the unsaturated linear branch, the region of recursive feasibility of DeePC without terminal ingredients, and the maximal control invariant set of admissible histories. We show these sets are nested and provide numerical examples.
☆ Counterfactual Screening of Rare Secondary Overloads in Power Grids with a Stochastic Surrogate for Electromagnetic Transient Simulations
Ayrton Almada, Laurent Pagnier, Igal Goldshtein, Michael, Chertkov
Power-system operators continually ask what would happen if a component failed now. Single-phase-to-ground faults cleared by single-pole tripping and automatic reclosure usually have no lasting consequences. In rare cases, however, the transient excited during the open-phase interval drives distant lines or transformers into overload that persists after the faulted line is restored. We develop a counterfactual screening framework for these secondary overloads, combining a linear stochastic swing surrogate with cross-entropy importance sampling. The surrogate represents the open-phase corridor through an effective coupling factor and localized multiplicative noise, with both parameters learned from electromagnetic-transient (EMT) simulations rather than prescribed. Closed-form propagation of the mean and covariance permits deterministic calibration without Monte Carlo sampling. On the reduced WECC 240-bus system, a globally calibrated model substantially improves finite-time agreement with the EMT electromechanical state. The global models are calibrated at reclosure and tested on disjoint faulted lines under a longer open-phase interval. Line- and operating-state-specific models use additional reclosure data from the assessment lines and provide smaller further gains at the cost of more separate fits. The fitted coupling is lower than the phase-counting baseline, consistent with the direction anticipated by sequence-network analysis. Cross-entropy importance sampling directs computational effort toward contingencies associated with persistent overload and yields rare-event probability estimates together with a map linking initiating faults to the elements they endanger. By separating offline EMT calibration from repeated surrogate evaluation, the method supports probabilistic contingency screening and identifies where detailed high-fidelity assessment is most valuable.
comment: 25 pages, 12 figures, 5 Tables, 1 Algorithm
☆ Learning Advantage Function Surrogates via Convex Conjugate Matching
Alvaro Maggiar
A policy trained to make per-unit decisions, such as how much of a product to order, tells us the best action but not the cost of deviating from it. That cost, the advantage function, is what downstream systems need when they have to depart from the per-unit optimum: to estimate the impact of ordering more or fewer units, to respond to a one-off vendor discount, or to satisfy a shared capacity constraint. The advantage function is what makes such trade-offs computable, yet pure policy-learning algorithms often produce the policy alone, without a critic that would yield it. We propose a method to train an advantage function surrogate through price perturbations motivated by a Fenchel-Young loss. We describe a two-stage recipe (fit the policy, then the cost model) and illustrate it on a multi-period inventory management problem.
☆ Radar Waveform Design via Convex Semidefinite Relaxation
Samuel Pinilla
The ambiguity function (AF) of a radar waveform describes its ability to resolve targets in range and Doppler. Designing a waveform that attains a prescribed AF magnitude is a phase retrieval problem with four trivial ambiguities, and a time- or band-limited pulse is determined up to these ambiguities by at most three times as many AF samples as it has time samples or frequencies. Existing solvers for the narrowband AF, however, are non-convex: they cannot guarantee that they reach the global minimizer, which is unique only up to the trivial ambiguities, so the recovered pulse depends on the starting point. This letter addresses this gap by lifting the problem to positive semidefinite matrices supported on the pulse band, where each AF sample becomes the magnitude of a linear functional. In the lifted space, recovery is formulated as a convex program, and a dual certificate provides a sufficient condition for exactness. The proposed algorithm, wavex, combines an initialization by relaxed reflections, convex semidefinite surrogate steps, and a local polish. Numerical experiments show that wavex accurately recovers band-limited pulses from complete AFs and from AFs with most of their samples removed, provided the remaining samples determine the pulse, and that its accuracy degrades gracefully as the noise increases. wavex is built on the open-source library invexapi, and the code that reproduces every result is available at https://github.com/samuelpinilla/waveX.

Under convexity and weighted summability of the primal stationarity errors, we prove boundedness of the primal-dual iterates and simultaneous $\mathcal O(k^{-2})$ last-iterate rates for the objective residual and constraint violation. Under strict parameter conditions, the primal-dual sequence converges to a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker pair, and both residuals improve to $o(k^{-2})$. These results require no strong convexity of the objective or constraints. Numerical experiments examine the performance of the proposed methods.

☆ Quadrature-Induced Local Minima in Structure-Preserving Lotka-Volterra Control

Harvest quadrature can change a discrete optimal control problem even when the state scheme stays fixed. We study this effect for a positivity-preserving Lotka--Volterra scheme. The difference appears in a model with harvesting alone: rewarding the scheme's removal flux gives a strictly convex reduced cost, whereas using prey density at the start of each step overestimates harvest and can create negative curvature and a strict local minimum that is not global. Rational root isolation certifies the two-step global minimizers. With diffusion in one space dimension, nonnegative bounded $H^1$ initial data and positive diffusivities, the costs, weighted gradients and Hessians differ by $O(τ)$ uniformly in the spatial mesh, where $τ$ is the time step. A uniform positive lower bound on the reduced Hessian gives the same order for the distance between nearby controls. A large enough effort penalty gives unique global discrete minimizers. We also prove positivity, exact population balance and a common variational limit, and derive exact discrete adjoints and Hessian actions. Numerical tests trace changes in curvature and stationary controls across parameters and grids, with costs evaluated on a common reference using adaptive time stepping. The construction extends to weighted production--destruction systems, giving exact harvest accounting and smooth derivatives on fixed grids.

☆ An abstract observability criterion via translation hulls, with applications to transport systems
Yacouba Simpore
We establish an observability criterion for translation-covariant families of operators on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$. Under continuity of the observed cell energies, a common summable localization bound, and reconstruction up to a locally collectively compact error, observability is equivalent to the absence of nonzero uniformly local invisible states on every configuration in the full translation hull. For one-dimensional transport systems satisfying the Kalman rank condition, this yields localized observability in the intrinsic Kalman--Jordan energy space for arbitrary real Jordan structure and nonzero speeds. For unions of observed intervals with a uniform positive lower length bound, the sharp condition is that the slowest characteristic travels farther than the gap supremum. Observability fails at equality even when this supremum is not attained. Duality gives exact controllability in the dual energy space. We also obtain sharp criteria for translating observation regions and scalar transport with an integrable convolution kernel. The reconstruction hypothesis is also necessary for observability. An anisotropic heat-flux example shows that it applies beyond coercive multiplication-plus-compact Gramian decompositions.
☆ Communication-Efficient Distributionally Robust Federated Averaging with Multi-Source Data
Yingzhu Liu, Zhongkui Li, Pengcheng You, Ashish Cherukuri
Federated learning trains a shared model from distributed client data. The deployment risk is typically specified through two approximations: each unknown local distribution is replaced by its empirical distribution, and the unknown deployment mixture across clients is replaced by empirical or prescribed training weights. Existing robust methods usually address one approximation at a time through local distributional ambiguity sets or worst-case client mixtures. However, joint treatment of both approximations remains underexplored. To address this gap, we construct a global ambiguity set formed by admissible mixtures of client-wise Wasserstein ambiguity sets, yielding a distributionally robust optimization formulation. The construction allows client-dependent ambiguity radii, preserves client-wise separability of the objective function, and yields a high-probability out-of-sample guarantee for the resulting robust problem. We then introduce a penalty-based approximation of this formulation and develop a communication-efficient algorithm called BiDRO-FedAvg, for which we establish a convergence guarantee. We validate the proposed framework through a market-demand prediction simulation.

We study the terminal controllability of the three-dimensional acoustic wave equation driven by finitely many fixed point sources, with zero initial data and time-dependent amplitudes supported in a finite interval. Although finitely many fixed sources cannot control the whole energy space, we establish the following results: (i) For source amplitudes in the first-order Sobolev space in time, the terminal state has finite energy if and only if all amplitudes vanish at both endpoints of the control interval. (ii) We derive an exact frequency-domain identity for the terminal energy involving a Gram matrix whose diagonal entries are one and whose off-diagonal entries are given by the sinc function, depending on frequency and source separation. (iii) For every positive control time, the terminal control operator is bounded below and is an isomorphism onto its closed reachable range, which has infinite codimension even among states satisfying the finite-propagation support condition. (iv) We establish a necessary and sufficient radiation-field criterion for reachability, provide stable reconstruction of the unique controls, and characterize the best approximation of non-reachable targets. The optimal coercivity constant equals one before the shortest source travel time. At long times, it decays as the inverse square of the control time for two sources and as the inverse fourth power for three equally spaced collinear sources. We also obtain upper bounds for general configurations and illustrate the theoretical results through reproducible Galerkin computations.

In this paper we study the linearization of nonautonomous differential inclusions, whose right-hand side is integrably Lipschitz in the state variable and measurable in time. We establish measurability results for time-dependent graphs and identify the Clarke tangent cone to the set of their measurable selections in $L^\infty\times L^1$. Combining this characterization with a subtransversality argument, we obtain a lower estimate for the Clarke tangent cone to the set of all admissible trajectories starting from a fixed set. As an application, we give sufficient conditions for local controllability around a closed terminal set.

Deep hashing encodes high-dimensional image features into compact binary codes, enabling efficient similarity search in large-scale content-based image retrieval, a problem akin to semantic-preserving lossy compression under extreme bit-rate constraints. A fundamental challenge in deep hashing stems from the discrete nature of quantization in generating the codes. W-type regularizations, such as $z\mapsto\||z|-1\|_1$, are widely adopted and empirically effective at pushing network outputs toward binary values. However, existing methods often directly optimize these regularizations without convergence guarantees. While proximal gradient methods offer a promising solution, the coupling between W-type regularizers and neural network outputs results in composite forms that generally lack closed-form proximal solutions. In this paper, using Fenchel duality, we reformulate the nonconvex W-type regularization term through its convex conjugate, yielding a min-max problem with tractable proximal updates. We show that this min-max problem captures the stationarity of the original deep hashing objective up to the quantization error. Building on this problem, we present a stochastic primal-dual hashing algorithm, referred to as DualHash, with oracle complexity guarantees. We derive two algorithm instances: a momentum-based version with $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$ oracle complexity and an improved $O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ version using variance reduction, both for $\varepsilon$-KKT points of the min-max problem, which yield near-stationarity guarantees for the original objective. Experiments on three standard datasets demonstrate competitive retrieval accuracy and reduced quantization error, validating the practical value of DualHash for image retrieval problems. Our implementation of DualHash is available at https://github.com/RailLee/DualHash.

♻ ☆ Bellman-sufficient Information Complexity
Yunbei Xu
We introduce Bellman-sufficient information complexity for minimax analysis of sequential decision problems. A Bellman-sufficient state retains the history needed for the controlled recursion; an index $Y=χ(Ω)$ specifies which information the bounds charge. A log-penalized Bellman program gives the upper bound, and a Bellman--Fano comparison with an algorithm-dependent reference trajectory gives the lower bound. When admissibility, calibration, and growth conditions hold and the bounds match at a common localization scale, they yield an information-risk sandwich. UCB bounds the immediate decision loss through calibration and optimism, while AMS/EBO gives a robust relaxation of the AIR Bellman program. Our main application gives a negative answer to a widely studied form of the GP--UCB minimax-optimality question. For every $0<α<1/4$, we construct a fixed bounded continuous kernel with minimax regret $Θ(T^{1-α})$ along an infinite sequence of horizons. At those horizons, two globally calibrated GP--UCB rules incur linear regret under one fixed truth. A policy that applies action-index AMS to a predetermined finite set in each epoch attains the minimax order; EBO gives a dual interpretation. Many low-value directions inflate the global exploration multiplier even though ignoring them is inexpensive. Through the canonical RKHS feature map, the same construction gives a finite-horizon polynomial minimax gap for the specified maximal-information-calibrated LinUCB rule. A numerical experiment illustrates the mechanism.
♻ ☆ On the Stability Connection Between Discrete-Time Algorithms and Their Resolution ODEs: Applications to Min-Max Optimisation
Amir Ali Farzin, Yuen-Man Pun, Philipp Braun, Iman Shames
We establish a connection between the stability of discrete-time algorithms (DTAs) and continuous-time dynamical systems, in particular their $O(s^r)$-resolution ordinary differential equations (ODEs). We show that exponential stability of a common equilibrium transfers to the DTA whenever the one-step error is small relative to the distance to the equilibrium and the one-step Lyapunov decay. This condition is sharp in order, and one-step consistency alone is insufficient. The result is local and allows step-size-dependent ODEs and Lyapunov functions, covering $O(s)$-resolution ODEs whose decay rate vanishes as the step size tends to zero. Asymptotic stability is not inherited in general, but a comparison criterion and a checkable compatibility condition ensure it carries over for equilibria and compact sets. For resolution ODEs, joint regularity of the update map guarantees the required error bound. We apply the framework to two-timescale gradient descent ascent (TT-GDA), generalised extragradient, two-timescale proximal point, and (regularised) damped Newton, showing that for small step sizes and suitable parameters, every saddle point with invertible Hessian is locally exponentially stable for all but TT-GDA. For degenerate saddle points, the framework yields asymptotic stability and convergence rates.
♻ ☆ Quadratic Mean-Field BSDEs and Exponential Utility Maximization
Yining Ding, Kihun Nam, Jiaqiang Wen
In this paper, we study a class of real-valued mean-field backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) with generators of quadratic growth in the control variable and the mean-field term. For bounded terminal conditions satisfying suitable structural regularity, we establish existence and uniqueness under two complementary quadratic regimes; the uniformly continuous path-dependent case additionally requires a uniform quadratic bound on the normalized generator. Our approach for these results combines Malliavin calculus with refined BMO and stability estimates, and bridges the gap between the quadratic BSDE results of [Ann. Probab. 45 (2017), pp. 3795--3828] and [Ann. Appl. Probab. 35 (2025), pp. 2128--2174]. Motivated by a mean-field exponential utility maximization problem, we further extend our framework to terminal conditions without imposing continuity or Markovian structure on the terminal condition. Under a suitable smallness condition on the oscillation of the terminal value around its mean, the associated quadratic BSDE admits a unique solution in a suitable small solution class. We then apply the extended theory to solve a mean-field exponential utility maximization problem, thereby extending the constrained exponential utility framework of Hu et al. [Ann. Appl. Probab. 15 (2005), pp. 1691--1712] to a mean-field setting.

We establish dual representation and stability results for multimarginal optimal transport (MOT) with bounded continuous costs. Our approach uses mutually $c$-conjugate potentials: each component is the largest function compatible with the dual constraint when the others are fixed. A single sweep of successive component updates produces such a family from any real-valued feasible family while preserving contact points. The resulting potentials are bounded and upper semicontinuous. On fixed compact metric spaces, normalization at fixed reference points yields a compact class of continuous potentials in the product uniform norm. This class is independent of the marginals and contains a dual maximizer for every marginal tuple. We prove its Lipschitz dependence on the cost in Hausdorff distance. Under uniform cost convergence and weak marginal convergence, transport values converge. The corresponding normalized optimizer sets are upper stable in the product uniform norm, without uniqueness assumptions. We also obtain value bounds in total variation and, for coordinatewise Lipschitz costs, Wasserstein distance. For coordinatewise Lipschitz reference costs, a power-growth condition on the dual objective gives one-sided Hölder estimates for optimizer sets under joint perturbations. On finite spaces, polyhedral structure yields linear growth and one-sided Lipschitz estimates with reference-dependent constants. On Polish spaces, total boundedness of the coordinate cost profiles in the uniform norm yields a compact normalized representation. For a fixed cost satisfying this condition, value continuity and upper stability of normalized conjugate optimizer sets hold under weak marginal convergence.

We study the standard form Integer Programming problem (IP) parametrized by the imbalanced circuit packing number. This number is $0$ if and only if $A$ can be transformed to a totally unimodular matrix by row operations, in which case (IP) is solvable in polynomial time. We show that if the constraint matrix represents a graphic matroid, (IP) is fixed-parameter tractable when parametrized by the imbalanced circuit packing number of the matrix. The proof combines an Erdős-Pósa property for edge-colored non-monochromatic cycles with a reduction to mixed-integer programming using few integer variables. In contrast, by a reduction from the parity potential problem, we show NP-completeness of feasibility of (IP) when the constraint matrix represents a cographic matroid, even if kernel of the constraint matrix is $2$-regular and imbalanced circuits pairwise intersect.
♻ ☆ The Shadow Price of Intelligence: Quality Degradation and Retry Feedback in LLM Inference

Large language model providers are compute constrained, and a common response to congestion is to degrade service: route queries to smaller models, cut reasoning budgets, or shorten context windows. A user who receives an unsatisfactory answer either retries, adding load while the system is busy, or abandons, possibly as churn. We model inference serving as a control problem in which service quality is the provider's decision. A two-regime fluid approximation with retries folded into the service rate gives closed-form trajectories and crossing times, so the dynamic program over quality tiers needs no simulation. We characterize a region in which a weaker tier uses less energy per task but more capacity per task, and show that in the fluid model reactive throttling to such a tier can keep the queue from draining. With heterogeneous customers the problem is a transportation problem with retry-inflated capacity coefficients; optimal routing follows a $cμ$-type index, and the dual of the capacity constraint gives the marginal cost of one more query by class and time. We illustrate the method on five instances calibrated to public benchmark data.

♻ ☆ Real-Time Dynamic N-1 Screening: Identifying High-Risk Lines and Transformers After Common Faults
Ayrton Almada, Laurent Pagnier, Igal Goldshtein, Saif R. Kazi, Michael, Chertkov
Power system operators routinely perform N-1 contingency analysis, yet conventional tools provide limited guidance on which lines or transformers deserve heightened attention during fast post-fault transients. In particular, static screening does not reveal whether (1) the same faulted line repeatedly triggers severe downstream overloads, or (2) a specific transformer emerges as vulnerable across many distinct fault scenarios. This paper introduces a real-time dynamic N-1 screening framework that addresses this gap by estimating, for each counterfactual single-phase transmission fault, the probability of transient overcurrent on critical grid elements. The output is an operator-facing dashboard that ranks (a) faulted lines whose outages most frequently lead to dangerous transformer overloads, and (b) transformers that consistently overload across top-risk scenarios, both of which are actionable indicators for real-time situational awareness. The approach models post-fault electromechanical dynamics using a linear stochastic formulation of the swing equations with short-lived, fault-localized uncertainty, and combines analytic transient evaluation with cross-entropy based importance sampling to efficiently estimate rare but high-impact events. All N-1 contingencies are evaluated in parallel with linear computational complexity. The framework is demonstrated on the IEEE 118-bus system, where it reveals latent high-risk lines and transformers that remain invisible under deterministic dynamic or static N-1 analysis. Results show orders-of-magnitude computational speedup relative to brute-force Monte Carlo, enabling practical deployment within real-time operational cycles.

♻ ☆ A Direction Adaptation Evolution Strategy for Noisy Derivative-Free Optimization
Morteza Kimiaei, Mahsa Yousefi
In noisy derivative-free optimization (DFO), methods based on the matrix adaptation evolution strategy (MAES) often mistakenly identify points with spuriously good function values, undermining selection and leading to unreliable search directions. To address this, we develop a novel direction adaptation evolution strategy (DAES) that targets the algorithmic phases prone to noise propagation, combining selected-population search with complexity analysis. Fixing the transformation matrix to the identity, DAES employs a structured direction-generation mechanism consisting of symmetric sampling, joint sorting--selection of noisy values, partitioning of all sampled directions into three ranked groups, and construction of a heuristic search direction. Along this direction, a noisy derivative-free sufficient descent condition with extrapolation is applied. Using a probabilistic angle condition preserved through our proposed framework, we obtain, to the best of our knowledge, the first high-probability evaluation-complexity bounds for a noisy MAES-type method across nonconvex, convex, and strongly convex objectives, under bounded noise. Finally, experiments on 230 BARON BCP problems across eight noise levels compare DAES with five DFO solvers, notably MADFO, showing greater robustness at intermediate-to-small budgets.

♻ ☆ Kalman structure and observability for transport systems
Yacouba Simpore
We study observability and controllability for constant-coefficient first-order hyperbolic systems on the real line when only part of the state is observed or controlled. Even when the Kalman rank condition holds, the usual \(L^2(\mathbb R)^N\)-observability estimate may fail because some components are detected only through the dynamics. We show that the Kalman structure determines the appropriate observability estimate. A component that becomes visible after \(k\) algebraic steps is measured at low Fourier frequencies with a weight of order \(|ξ|^{2k}\) in the Fourier variable. This yields a natural Kalman-adapted observation space for the system. Assuming that the transport matrix \(A\) is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb R\), we prove whole-line observability in this space for every positive time and derive exact controllability in the corresponding dual space. If, in addition, \(A\) has no zero eigenvalue and the observation set satisfies the one-dimensional bounded-gap condition, we establish localized observability whenever the observation time exceeds the natural characteristic travel-time threshold. Separately, in the whole-line setting, we extend the construction to transport matrices \(A\) with real spectrum and possible nontrivial Jordan blocks.
♻ ☆ Quantale-Enriched Co-Design: Toward a Framework for Quantitative Heterogeneous System Design
Hans Riess, Yujun Huang, Matthew Klawonn, Gioele Zardini, Matthew Hale
Monotone co-design enables compositional engineering design by modeling components as feasibility relations between required resources and provided functionalities. However, its boolean formulation cannot natively represent quantitative criteria such as cost, confidence, or implementation choice. In practice, these considerations are introduced through ad-hoc scalarization or by augmenting the resource space, which obscures system structure and increases computational complexity. Therefore, we develop a quantale-enriched theory of co-design in which resources and functionalities are quantale-enriched categories and design problems are quantale-enriched profunctors, which lifts co-design from boolean feasibility to quantitative evaluation. Series, parallel, and feedback composition remain valid over any commutative quantale, and change-of-base maps between quantales yield heterogeneous composition, so that subsystems evaluated in different local semantics can be composed in a common framework. Numerical examples on a target-tracking system and a UAV delivery problem demonstrate this framework and show how it avoids the drawbacks of boolean-only formulations.

We establish reformulations of these problems as linear optimization over the product of the CP cone and the copositive (COP) cone, namely, the COP-CP programs. A hierarchy of coupled Moment-SOS type semidefinite relaxations is proposed to solve these COP-CP programs. We show that this approach has asymptotic convergence under mild assumptions. Moreover, we use the coupled flat truncation conditions (FTCs) to certify tightness of semidefinite relaxations, and we give sufficient conditions for finite convergence of the hierarchy, under which the FTCs hold at every optimal solution of all sufficiently high-order relaxations. Numerical experiments are presented to show the effectiveness of our method.

We consider the Lasserre hierarchy for computing bounds on the stability number of graphs. The semidefinite programs (SDPs) arising from this hierarchy involve large matrix variables and many linear constraints, which makes them difficult to solve using interior-point methods. We propose solving these SDPs using the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). When the second level of the Lasserre hierarchy for a given graph is intractable for the ADMM, we consider an intermediate-level relaxation of the hierarchy. To warm-start the ADMM, we use an optimal solution from the first level of the Lasserre hierarchy, which is equivalent to the well-known Lovász theta function. Additionally, we use this solution to determine which degree two monomials to add in the Lasserre hierarchy relaxation to obtain an intermediate level between 1 and 2. Computational results demonstrate that our approach yields strong bounds on the stability number, which are computable within reasonable running times. We provide {improved} bounds on the stability number of various graphs from the literature.
♻ ☆ Boundary Collisions and Weak Excitation in LQR Policy-Gradient Flows

Closed-loop stability concerns all initial states, whereas an LQR cost evaluates only the directions excited by a prescribed initial-state distribution. We study how this distinction affects Euclidean policy-gradient flows. For every nonzero deficient covariance rank, we construct relatively open families of controllable data and open sets of stabilizing initial gains whose exact gradient trajectories reach the stability boundary in finite optimization time. The state Gramian can remain positive definite at every time before collision. By separating the cost contribution of a critical mode, we obtain a local collision criterion based on direction attraction and motion toward the stability boundary. Adding excitation of strength $\varepsilon$ yields matching $Θ(\sqrt\varepsilon)$ bounds on the local minimum stability margin for trajectories that would otherwise collide. For a class of single-input, corank-one systems, these bounds hold over the entire trajectory without a common compact-set assumption. Numerical examples further illustrate the dynamics and scaling laws.
♻ ☆ On the Complexity of Finding Stationary Points in Stochastic $(L_0, L_1)$-Smooth Nonconvex Optimization

We study the stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) complexity of finding $ε$-stationary points of $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth nonconvex functions. We resolve this question for an unbiased SFO whose gradient noise has a $p$th central moment bounded by $σ^p$ for some $σ\geq 0$, where $p\in(1,2]$.Specifically, we establish an SFO lower bound of $Ω\big(\big(σ^{\frac{p}{p-1}}ε^{-\frac{p}{p-1}}+1\big) (L_0 Δε^{-2}+L_1Δε^{-1})\big)$, where $Δ>0$ is the initial optimality gap.This bound identifies an unavoidable contribution proportional to $L_1ε^{-1}Δ$. We also prove that mini-batch (smoothed) normalized SGD can attain a matching upper bound, thereby establishing the optimal SFO complexity.
comment: Strengthened the SFO lower bound under a less restrictive accuracy condition. Added an impossibility result for finite-sum optimization under individual $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness. Revised proofs and improved presentation
♻ ☆ LEAF: A Learning-Enabled ADMM Framework for Accelerated Convex Optimization
Binh Nguyen, Trinh Tran, Truong X. Nghiem
We propose LEAF, a learning-enabled ADMM framework for accelerated convex optimization. The key idea is to approximate the Moreau envelope of the objective function using an Input Convex Neural Network (ICNN), resulting in a learned model that preserves convexity and smoothness. This leads to the proposed Moreau Envelope Learning ADMM (MEL-ADMM) and its splitting variant sMEL-ADMM. Unlike existing approaches that learn high-dimensional operators directly, LEAF learns a scalar-valued Moreau envelope, significantly reducing model complexity and improving data efficiency. The framework accommodates a broad class of convex problems with smooth and non-smooth objectives. By embedding convexity explicitly through the ICNN architecture, the proposed approach maintains high approximation accuracy while preserving key structural properties of the optimization problem. Both MEL-ADMM and sMEL-ADMM are developed with theoretical guarantees of convergence and feasibility under the learned model. Rigorous analysis shows that the proposed methods achieve convergence rates comparable to classical ADMM while reducing per-iteration computational cost. Numerical experiments demonstrate up to an order-of-magnitude speedup over state-of-the-art solvers while maintaining low optimality gaps
♻ ☆ Adaptive direct search for blackbox optimization
Charles Audet, Théo Denorme, Youssef Diouane, Sébastien Le Digabel, Christophe Tribes
Two families of directional direct search methods have emerged in derivative-free and blackbox optimization (DFO and BBO), each based on distinct principles: Mesh Adaptive Direct Search (MADS) and Sufficient Decrease Direct Search (SDDS). MADS restricts trial points to a mesh and accepts any improvement, ensuring that none are missed, but at the cost of restricting the placement of trial points. SDDS allows greater freedom by evaluating points anywhere in the space, but accepts only those yielding a sufficient decrease in the objective function value, which may lead to discarding promising points. This work introduces a new class of methods, Adaptive Direct Search (ADS), which uses a novel acceptance rule based on the so-called punctured space, avoiding both mesh and sufficient decrease conditions. ADS enables flexible search while addressing the limitations of MADS and SDDS, and retains the theoretical foundations of directional direct search. Computational results in constrained and unconstrained settings highlight its performance compared to both MADS and SDDS.

The identification of valid inequalities, such as the rounded capacity inequalities (RCIs), is a key component of cutting plane methods for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP). While a deep learning-based separation method can learn to find high-quality cuts, our analysis reveals that the model produces fewer cuts than expected because it is insufficiently sensitive to generate a diverse set of generated subsets. This paper proposes an alternative: enhancing the performance of a trained model at inference time through a new test-time search with stochasticity. First, we introduce stochastic edge selection into the graph coarsening procedure, replacing the previously proposed greedy approach. Second, we propose the Graph Coarsening History-based Partitioning (GraphCHiP) algorithm, which leverages coarsening history to identify not only RCIs but also, for the first time, the Framed capacity inequalities (FCIs). Experiments on randomly generated CVRP instances demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in reducing the dual gap compared to the existing neural separation method. Additionally, our method discovers effective FCIs on a specific instance, despite the challenging nature of identifying such cuts.
